145. Emigration into the Bombay Presidency.—Passing over Bilodiistan, which has already been discussed, the next Province which marches with our territories is Sindh. Col. 90 of Table XI gives figures for
Bombay, while col. 97 gives others for Sindh. But some divisional offices, following the letter of the Census
orders, did not separate the two ; and indeed, according to the Government of India instructions the two were
not to be distinguished in the schedules, and therefore it is not safe to take the figures separately. It will
be seen from Abstract No. 23 that, -while only 4,780 persons have emigrated from Bombay to the Panjab,
no fewer than 35,379 have left the Panjab for Bombay, of whom 29,316 are to be found in Sindh ; and that
the proportion of males is far higher among the emigrants than among the immigrants, and is indeed quite
exceptionally high as compared with other Provinces, being however, as would naturally be expected, lower
in Sindh than in the more distant parts of the Presidency. I am not at all certain as to the explanation of
this enormous emigration. The figures for immigration afford us no clue, since the immigrants from Bombay
would appear to be chiefly mercantile, being collected for the most part at Amritsar, Lahore, Rawalpindi,
Multan, and Peshawar. The immigrants from Sindli are chiefly to be found in Bahawalpur (under the head
Bombay) and Derah Ghazi Khan, the two portions of our territory which border on Sindh. I had at first
thought that much of the emigration must be
of old standing, and have taken place duringthe troubles which accompanied the siege of

hr/s taken place within the last few years, was also controlled by the Government of the Panjab. I have
K-fttle doubt that the emigration from Panjdb British Territory into Sindh consists chiefly of establishment
/connected with the Indus Valley Railway, and of gangs of workmen employed on the Kandahar and Sibi
r
line. But another cause is doubtless to be found in the large number of Sikhs resident in Sindh, the only
part of India except the Panjab in which Sikhs are to be found in any numbers, though I shall explain in
the next chapter that they are probably not all true Sikhs in the sense in which we understand the term.
Mr. Baines, the Bombay Census Officer, who has most kindly given me his opinion on the question, points
out that "there is a natural tendency for this (the Sikh) class to import wives and shop-keepers from the
" place which, as nearer their religious home, is more honourably regarded than their native village or town."
The emigration from Native States is probably almost wholly from Bahawalpur. It may doubtless have been
promoted by the troubles already alluded t o ; but even without any such special cause, the contrast
between what was, till we took it over in 1867, the most backward, and is still the most unfertile of our
Native States, and the trans-Indus plains of Sindh is probably sufficient to explain the migration. A
large portion of the Bahawalpur territory consists of rolling prairies similar to those of northern Rajputana; and like that Province, and unlike the remainder of the Western Plains of the Panjab, suffers terribly from famine, and especially so suffered in the famine of 1868. Thus we find that, while Bahawalpur has a total population of under 525,000 souls, no fewer than 25,600 have emigrated during the
present generation to British Territory, almost entirely to those of our districts which adjoin the State.
Of the remaining emigrants to the Bombay Presidency, excluding Sindh, more than half are to be found
in the city of Bombay itself.

the Bagar or tract adjoining our border is a rolling .prairie of sandy soil covered by scanty grass and with
an eminently precarious rainfall, and the agriculture is so primitive that the people have not yet risen to the
conception of growing two crops in the same year, the autumn crop alone being cultivated, though the

The fact is that when we once leave the neighbourhood of
the Jamna, a very large portion indeed of the immigrants from
the North-West consist of what we call in the Panjab Purdias, or low-caste men, mostly I believe
Chamars and Jaiswaras, who have come into the Province as camp-followers with troops from downcountry, many of them probably when the Panjab was first occupied:. Many of these men have settled
down permanently; and at places where there has once been a large cantonment, as at Karnai, will still
be found in considerable numbers. But many of them follow the troops from one cantonment to another,
or find other employment. In the east of the Panjab the stable servants are Purbias almost as a matter
of course. The figures of Table VI show how, outside the Dehli division, these immigrants from the NorthWest are almost confined to districts in which troops other than the Panjab Frontier Force are cantoned.
Many of the gangs of navvies, Ods, and the like, who wander in search of emplovment on earthwork through
the length and breadth of the Province also hail from the North-West. But'the mass of the immigration
into the Dehli division, Ambala, and Rohtak, which districts include 57 per cent, of the whole, is reciprocal, as is shown by the sex-figures quoted above : though in Ambala and Dehli the presence of cantonments,
and in the latter the attractions of. a great centre of trade, have doubtless caused a great deal of immigra&
tion of both the permanent and temporary types.

153- Figures for intra-provincial details.—I now turn to migration within the Province—or, to
use more exact language, to the intra-provincial details of migration. I propose to discuss the direction
and amount of migration to and from the various districts and states. But to do this with any approach
to accuracy, we cannot altogether neglect emigration beyond the limits of the Province. Now we know
the exact number of people (see Abstract No. 23), who have emigrated from the Panjab to each of the
other Indian Provinces; but unfortunately we do not know from what part of the Panjab they have come.
Some sort of estimate therefore becomes necessary. Emigration to countries beyond the Indian empire
may, as I have already pointed out, be neglected ; and the emigration to Provinces which do not march
with the Panjab is so small in extent, and probably so much distributed over the several districts, that
it is not necessary to take it into account. But where other Provinces march with ours, and especially
in the east where reciprocal migration is extensive, it is necessary to form an estimate of the emigration from each district across our frontier. It would be absurd to compare the emigration from Rohtak to
the districts which surround it on all sides with that from Dehli, if we excluded from the latter the movement across nearly half its border where it marches with the North-West Provinces. I have therefore
framed a rough estimate of the numbers of each sex who may be supposed to have emigrated from the
several border districts to the Provinces upon which they touch, and this estimated emigration has
been included in the figures 1 shall presently discuss. It is necessary that it should be known, for the
purposes of the next Census report, if for no other, how I have arrived at my estimate; and 1 therefore
give details below in small type. The figures for intra-provincial migration are contained in the following tables. Table XI, Appendices A and B, shows the distribution by birth-place of the population of each
district and state in the Province, and consequently the distribution by residence of the immigrants from
each state, district, province, and country, whether within or beyond the Panjab. Supplementary Table
F, Appendix C, shows gain or loss by migration in each district. Supplementary Tables G and H show
the movements of the population from district to district, while Supplementary Tables C, D, and E give
details of birth-place.
154. North-West Provinces.—See the discussion on the migration from those provinces in sections 140, 150 above. The NorthWest P r o v i n c e Census tables give ns figures for totaWunigration from the P a n j a b ; but unfortunately give no details of the districts
in which t h e e emigrants are to be found. Such details would have rendered the estimate easy and certain. J t is probable t h a t
there is b u t little emigration from the P a n j a b to balance the immigration of camp-followers and the like, as the conditions which
have caused ibis immigration act in one direction o n l y ; t h a t the greater part of the emigration has taken place from the four
districts which march with the N o r t h - W e s t ; and that these districts have furnished a larger proportion of t h e female than of the
male e m i " r a " t s , as t h e migration will have been to a great extent reciprocal. The figures which the N o r t h - W e s t Provinces
tables give for immigration from " o t h e r parts of I n d i a " into their several districts tend to support this conclusion. The total immigration" from the North-West Provinces into the four border districts is males 5 3 , 1 8 3 ; females 76,667. The total emigration from
P a n j a b British Territory into t h e N o r t h - W e s t Provinces is males 67,303 ; females 72,499.
Assuming t h a t 80 per •cent, of the male and 90 per cent, of t h e female emigrants go from the four districts, and d i s t r i b u t i n g
this portion of the emigration among them in proportion to the
female immigration into each, t h a t being the best, standard of reciprocal migration—first, however, reducing the female immigration

It is not prima fade to be wondered at that the emigration from British Territory to Native States
should be large in the Pan jab. These States, or at any rate such of them as lie in the Eastern Plains, are
probably more advanced than any other Native States in India. They follow closely in our administrative
footsteps, they are subject to strict supervision the very consciousness of which renders interference
unnecessary, and their land revenue demand, if heavier) is at least more elastic than our own. It is an
open question whether the Governments of such States, follQ\ving our system in its best feat ur es but
departing from it where unsuitable to the genius of the people, kept by us in the broad path of general
justice and moderation but left to take their own way in all the details of administration, with smaller
charges and a less expensive staff than our own, and hampered by no refinements of occidental
State craft,-it is, I say, an open question whether such Governments, content to be as simple in their
system .as are the people whom they rule, are not at least as well suited to make their subjects happy
as is the cumbrous machinery of our Indian administration. What native rule is when unchecked and
unguided I have endeavoured to pout-tray in the first part of this chapter. But, given a good example
and a firm hand over them, such Governments as those of Our larger states) enjoying the advantage
of sympathy with their fellow-countrymen and an intuitive knowledge of their needs and capacities,
possess many of the merits and avoid many of the defects of our own system. And if Bahawalpu r and
the Hill States are in some respects less developed than their neighbours of the Eastern Plains, the former
had been under the direct management of our Government for the fifteen years before the Census) -vhikof the latter Chamba has been similarly administered by an En6"lish officer for the last nine "ears, Su kc t
had been under the direct control of the Commissioner of }alandhar since the deposition of Raja Rudra
Sen in 1878, while the Superintendent of Hill States at Simla exercises a paternal care cve r the
smaller states which is unknown to the more important feudatories.

attracted not only a certain number of permanent settlers in those parts, but also still more numerous
graziers whom the drought of the years immediately preceding the Census had driven down to the river
banks in search of pasture.
But there can be little doubt that much of the emigration and immigration respectively can be referred
to two different periods in the history of the State. Prior to the year 1866, when we took it under our
superintendence, Bahawalpur had suffered from mal-administration and rebellion almost amounting to
anarchy, and little or nothing had been done to modify the natural aridity of its plains. It is from this period
that much of the emigration probably dates. In 1866 an English Superintendent was appointed; in
1868, just as the famine began which raged with such severity in the neighbouring tracts of Rajputana,
large inundation canals were commenced ; and in six years from that date the area irrigated by canals
had nearly doubled, having increased from 336 to 617 square miles. Between 1868 1 and 1881 the population of Bahawalpur increased from 364,502 to 573,494, or by 58 per cent. ; and it is almost certain
that by far the greater part of the immigration has taken place during these last thirteen years.

F L U C T U A T I O N S .OF POPULATION".

L Chap. III.

Part II.—Migrations of the People.
reason for the distinction. In the first place the montane and sub-montane districts are already overcrowded,
and afford no room for immigrants from without. Below them stretch the Eastern Plains which, situated
between them and the arid and famine-scourged prairies of RAjputana, present in their river valleys,
their canal-irrigated dodbs, and their virgin pastures of moderate rainfall, every degree of fertility and
of .physical advantage to welcome the surplus population of the overcrowded districts, to attract the
inhabitants of the wastes to the south, and to tempt the people of one district to move into another. On
the other hand, in the sparsely peopled districts of the Western Plains the culturable portions are singularly
uniform in their physical characteristics. Each district has a certain riverain in which alone cultivation is
possible, and of which there is- still a sufficient portion uncultivated to afford ample room for the
expansion of its own population, and thus there is by comparison with the Eastern Plains but little inducement to migration from one district to another. Again the western districts are not subject to that
periodical recurrence of scarcity which ever and again drives the inhabitants of many of the eastern
districts, to wander from their homes, at first perhaps with the intention of returning, but often to
settle permanently in the spots where they first find relief. So too the western districts lie far away
from any densely peopled tract the surplus population of which might flow over into them, while their
physical qualities and the character of their inhabitants are not such as to invite immigration from
a distance. In the Salt-range and frontier tracts the people are too distinct from those of the Panj£b
proper to have any tendency to settle among them.
162. Within the two main divisions of the list, however, degrees are clearly observable. If the
Western Plains are more uniform in their physical attractions than are those of the east, the inducements
offered by the canal systems of Multdn, Montgomery, and Muzaffargarh put them well at the bottom of the
western districts. The enormous Pawindah immigration gives Derah Ismail a far lower place than it would
otherwise occupy; the temporary immigration attracted by the Railway and Canal works and the transport
arrangements on the route to Kabul similarly affects Rawalpindi, Jahlam, and Peshawar, especially in the male
figures; while the immigration of fugitives from the Kashmir famine, who appear to have left their women
behind them in the tracts immediately below the hills while the men went on further in search of work, bring
the districts on the Kashmir border lower in the figures for both sexes than in those for males only.
Finally, the enormous immigration into the rapidly developing districts of Sirsa, Hissar, and Firozpur places
them at the very bottom of the list, while reciprocal migration, most active in the Jamna zone, brings the
districts of that tract into the next lowest place on the list for both sexes, a position which they no longer
occupy in the list for males.
163. The figures for the urban population need not be discussed at any length. The military or commercial centres and the towns lying on the line of rail or in the great highways of trade contain a foreign
element often enormously large, while the towns of those districts which lie apart from the busy movement
of commerce or of armies have,almost as large a proportion of indigenous population as have the villages
by which they are surrounded. In Kohat and Pindi, where the greatest temporary activity prevailed at the
time of the Census, only some 40 per cent, of the urban population was indigenous, while in the secluded
districts of Jhang and Shahpur not 8 per cent, of it was foreign.
The figures for the sexes are given in columns 9 to 12 of the Abstract. As might be expected, the
proportion of indigenous females is far higher than that of males in the western districts, and far lower in
the Eastern Plains and sub-montane districts where reciprocal migration obtains, so far at least as the
rural population is concerned. Even among the urban population the same difference is to be observed,
though not in so marked a degree. The large proportion of strangers which the towns contain in comparison with the villages is most marked throughout the Province.
For the Native States I have not got out separate figures for urban and rural population, and I am
therefore compelled to treat them apart from districts. Abstract No. 33 below gives their figures, together
with those for the ten divisions for comparison.
Abstract No. 33, showing the Proportion of its Population indigenous to each State arranged in order

There is no need to discuss the figures in detail, as they generally bear out the remarks already made.
The Hill States with Bahawalpur come well at the top of the list; and the Eastern States, almost in the

Para. 164. T
Chap. III. J

F L U C T U A T I O N S OF

POPULATION.

Part II—Migrations of the People.
164. Effect of density of population upon migration.—The effect of density of population upon the
movements of the people is very strikingly shown by the figures of Abstract No. 34 on the opposite
page.
The natural tendency of population is to move in the direction of least pressure, or, other things being
equal, from a more to a less densely peopled tract. Now in this Abstract the districts are arranged in order
of density of population, and the figures in Roman type show gain to the district whose name is to the left
by exchange with and at the expense of that whose name is at the bottom of the table ; in other words, they
show the movement of population wherever it follows the course above indicated. The figures in italics
show movement in the reverse direction, the more densely gaining at the expense of the less densely populated district. It will be seen at a glance that, excluding the first vertical column which gives the'figures
for the wholly abnormal district of Simla, the mass of the movement follows the natural course. But there
are very striking exceptions. In the first place the density of population on total area means very little in
some of the Panjab) districts, which include large areas of practically uninhabitable mountain or steppe ; and
in such cases the figures showing the proportion of population to cultivated area, given in the extreme margin of the abstract, are more instructive 1 . Thus the actual pressure of population in proportion to the means
for its support, as distinguished from mere density on total area, is probably higher in" the hill districts of
Hushyarpur, Kangra, Gurdaspur, and Ambala in that order than in any other part of the Panjab ; and accordingly, if we except small figures, we find each of these four districts in order giving population to all
others.
165. Again a very striking point is brought out by an examination not only of these figures, but of
those also for the general intra-provincial migration, including Native States. On the one hand, such
excessive density of population as indicates actual pressure and overcrowding is invariably accompanied by
emigration; on the other, such excessive sparsity of population in comparison with the available culturabie
area as indicates plenty of good land to be had on easy terms, is invariably accompanied by immigration.
But directly we leave the two extremes of density and sparseness of population, and turn to those
tracts which are more moderately populated in proportion to their agricultural capacities, we find that the
movement of population between such tracts is determined, not so much by the relative density of their
population, as by the special attractions which they respectively offer to the cultivator, and that as a
matter of fact the tendency is rather to move towards the more thickly peopled tracts, which are naturally
those in which such attractions are greatest. Thus while the over-crowded montane and sub-montane
districts are sending out their surplus population as emigrants, and the rapidly developing tracts of Sirsa.
and Hissar are attracting immigrants, the movement of population in the districts of more moderate density
is towards the canal irrigated districts of Multan, Muzaffargarh, Dera Ghazi Khan, and Montgomery in
the west, towards the Satluj Valley and the irrigation works of Firozpur and the Bari Doa"b in the centre,
and towards the Jamna and its canal in the east of the Province, or from the less densely to the more
densely peopled tracts. The distress which has forced the people of Gurgaon to emigrate, the temporary
demand for labour in the Salt-range districts, and the general attraction exercised by military or commercial centres, explain all the remaining exceptions to the general rule of migration.
166. Gain and loss by migration.—Abstract No. 35 on page 78 shows the manner and degree in which
migration to and from the district or State has affected its population, the districts being arranged in order
of net gain.
The rapidly developing districts of Sirsa, Lahore, Hissar, Firozpur, and Multnn head the list, together
with Kohat, Peshawar, and Rawalpindi which lie on the route to Kabul, and Dcrah Ismail which forms
the Panjab depot of the pa-windahs. In all these cases the gain has been greater among males than among
females. The same is the case in Muzaffargarh, Banmi, Derah Ghaxi, J ah lam, and Hazara, which occupy
the middle of the list together with Dehb and Rohtak, the two most progressive of the Jamna districts, but
in which the female gain is greater than the male. Next follow the remaining districts of the Eastern
Plains, in which the gain has been chiefly to the female population ; while the tabic is completed by the
sub-montane districts which have all lost largely.by emigration, especially of males, and by the districts
of Jhang, Shahpur, and in a less degree of Montgomery, whose population has been attracted by the development of neighbouring tracts, and of Gurgaon where famine and disease have driven the people forth.
In all these cases the male population has naturally been the first to move.
167. Concentration of Population in the larger Towns.—Another important feature of the movement of the Panjab people is the tendency which they are now exhibiting, in common with those of
European countries, to congregate more and more in the larger towns. The only prooi I possess of this
tendency is the fact that the population of those towns has increased since the last Census far more rapidly
than that of the villages, while the population of the smaller towns has actually decreased in numbers ;
and this would seem to bring the subject under the head of increase and decrease discussed in
the next part of this chapter rather than under migration. But it is notorious that the death-rate
of our town population is quite abnormally high, far higher than that of the rural tracts; and the
insanatory conditions which produce this result can hardly fail to have their usual effect in reducing the
urban birth-rates; while the difference in sanitation between the larger cities with their more carefu'
administration, and the smaller and more neglected towns, can hardly be so great as very materially to
affect the rate of increase of population. Thus the ordinary excess of births over deaths cannot account
for the facts, and the explanation must be sought for in actual movement of population. Abstract No. 36
on page 78 shows the increase of population between 1868 and 1881 in towns arranged in groups according to size, the first part of the table giving the figures for each group separately, and the remaining part
of the abstract dealing with all towns taken together which contain more or less than a given population.
1
N O T E - — T h e figures for the distribution over culturabie area would have been [still more instructive had their basis been of a
satisfactory character. I have already explained in section 87 why those figures wholly fail, in many of the Panjab districts, to afford
Any indication of t h e available room for expansion of population.

towns in general, it is almost certain that they have left the smaller for the larger towns, and it 'is quite
certain that, from one source or the other, the larger towns have attracted to themselves a population out
of all comparison with that moving to their smaller rivals. The almost unbroken decrease in the figures
of columns 10 and 14, and the hardly less striking series of column 6 of the Abstract, show how strong
has been the set of population towards the large cities. There is no doubt that the development of our
Railway system has been a principal factor in effecting this movement, for as transport and communication become quicker, cheaper, and more easy, the minor centres of trade decline and the commercial
activity of the Province tends to concentrate itself in a few great marts 1 . Even the apparent exceptions
to the rule of uniform decrease which the figures of column 6 of the Abstract disclose are but exemplifications of the principle upon which the rule is based. Take, for instance, the towns of between 9,000 and
8,000 souls. A reference to Table XIX will show that of those twelve towns no fewer than eight are in
the west of the Panjab, where the towns are throughout smaller than in the Eastern Plains. In other words
they are the large towns of their neighbourhood ; and though they show a higher rate of increase than
larger towns lying in another part of the Province, yet if the comparison were made separately for the
two tracts they would fall into their proper place, and form no exception to the rule that laro-e towns
have increased more rapidly than small ones. The same considerations will be found to account for all
the apparent exceptions, which in fact only prove the rule.
169. The movement is almost wholly beneficial. As I have before remarked, the insanatory conditions of village life in the Panjab differ in degree only from those of town life, while the larger towns
are better cared for in this respect than are the smaller ones. Thus the superior healthiness of rustic
life which is so marked in European countries, may be said scarcely to exist in this Province. On the
other hand the absence of industries other than agricultural, and the consequent dependence of the oreat
mass of the people upon a rainfall which is, in the Panjab at least, eminently variable and precarious
and upon the produce of cultivation which cannot keep pace with the increase of population, constitute one of the greatest difficulties of Indian administration ; and though the distance in this respect
between India and England is so enormous that generations must pass away before that difficulty is
materially lessened, yet any tendency of the population to become more urban in its character must
possess peculiar importance. Already the great cities of the Panjab seem to be attracting to themselves the
surplus population of the rural tracts, and so helping to relieve that pressure of population which is even
now seriously felt in some portions of the Province, and will year by year make itself more apparent;
while the_ increasing concentration of the population in great commercial centres can hardly fail to be
accompanied by, or at. least to pave the way for, the creation of new or the develop™—1- ' uC CAIOI:„CT
industries, and the more elaborate organisation and division of labour.
170. Tendency of the rural population towards dicp c l sion.—At the same time there is observable among the rural population an equally beneficial tendency in the opposite direction, which, though not
represented in our figures owing to the system on which they are tabulated, is, I believe, no less in actual
operation throughout all those parts of the Province in which compact village communities attain considerable size 2 . I have, in section 71, attempted to show that the typical large village community inhabitino- a
single homestead surrounded by a common wall, owes its existence in part at least to the necessity of selfdefence. With the spread of order under British rule that necessity has been in great measure removed ;
and the people are beginning to spread over their fields, and rustic life to approach, though as vet only in a
very limited degree, the conditions which characterise it in England. As population increases with national
prosperity, cultivation extends and the standard of agricultural practice rises. The more distant fields
have now to be watched, while the more valuable staples require more manure and more constant labour
and attention. A hut is accordingly built in the fields, in which the cattle are kept and some of the
young men spend the night. Cultivation extends still further from the main homestead, more huts are
-built, till at last a small hamlet springs up occupied in turn by various members of the families who own
the surrounding land, while the outlying fields are dotted over with isolated buildings, many of which
are destined to become the nuclei of similar hamlets. The larger the area of the villages the stronger the
tendency to a dispersion of this sort. The process is but another instance of that spread of severalty and
growth of individual rights to which I havealready made allusion in discussing houses and families (Part IV,
Chap. II). Much has been written of the manner in which the Indian village community has survived the
crash of empires and emerged unchanged from centuries of anarchy and misrule, ft may be that it is
destined to succumb to the dissolving spell of peace and settled administration ; and that the very sternness of the conditions at whose powerlessness to break it down historians have wondered, supplied the
external pressure which kept it together, and the withdrawal of which will allow it to fall asunder by disintegration from within.

FLUCTUATIONS OF POPULATION.

Chap. III. J

Part II.'—Migrations of the People.
population, and more especially of the rural population, live and die in the district in which they were
born. In the eastern portion of the Panjab, where no physical obstacles bar the way, and where varying conditions, and in some parts pressure of population tempt the people to move, migration is more
common than in the west; but even there the movement seldom extends to any distance, and is generally
confined to crossing the border from one district or state into its neighbour. In the south-east of the Province the till lately almost uninhabited prairies of Hissa'r and Sirsa have tempted crowds of immigrants
from arid Rajputana and from the Native States to their north, while the population of the central plains
has also moved eastwards, northwards, and westwards towards the rivers and the canals which distribute
their waters. In Gurgaon distress has of late years driven the people to seek employment beyond the
limits of the district, while along the Western Jamna Canal the ravages of saline efflorescence have compelled many of the inhabitants to seek new lands in neighbouring tracts. The sub-montane districts have
a population more dense than their culturable urea can support in comfort, and their surplus numbers are
moving southwards into the river valleys, and even beyond them into the central plains, while the extension
of irrigation in Lahore and Firozpur has attracted a special immigration to those districts. Within the
mountains themselves the population is peculiarly stationary, the chief movement being a periodic descent
from the high ranges to the warmer valleys in the winter season, and an influx of labourers from Ladikh to
find work on our system of mountain roads.
172, In the Western Plains there is little pressure of population, distances are great, and the people
move but little. Yet the fertile plains of Sindh have attracted settlers in considerable numbers from Bahawalpur; the recent extension of inundation canals in the districts of Montgomery, Multan, Muzaffargarh, and
Derah Ghazi Khan and the State of Bahawalpur has drawn numerous immigrants from the neighbouring
districts and from Rajputana; and there are signs that, with the spread of order and the extension of
cultivation, the pastoral tribes of the central steppes are moving into the river valleys. This latter movement, however, is probably in some degree temporary, and due to the seasons of scanty rainfall.which preceded the Census and compelled the herds to move riverwards in search of pasture; and the same cause
accounts in part for the similar movement already remarked in the Eastern Plains. The people of the Saltrange Tract and of the frontier itself are a peculiar people, and mix but little with the inhabitants of the
Panjab proper; and were it not for the exceptional demand for labour created by the Kabul campaign
there would be but little movement between these two portions of the Province. But the tribes
of the Pathan border are gradually acquiring lands and settling in considerable numbers in British Territory, more especially in Bannu and Peshawar, while year by year as winter approaches the hill-men move
down to the Panjab plains to cultivate, to trade, or to work as labourers.^ So too with returning autumn the
great pawr.dah caravans scatter their agents over the Province while their herds pasture in the Indus Valley,
-.and t^-"~—*" of labourers from the far hills of Hazira beyond Kabul pour into the Panjab in search of
employment. The evil M f . . r 0 n f the native rule, and still more the terrible famine which has latelv
devastatedJCashmfr, have driven thouo a n ds of starving families into the Province, the women an':
children remaining in the districts on the bordei while the men have passed onwards to where labour «-as>
more in demand.
173. The women of the Panjab are naturally less inclined to emigrate than are the men, yet the
custom of the Eastern Plains which prescribes that brides shall be sought at a distance carries them in
numbers of villages grouped according to size in t h e enumerations of 1868 and 1881. T h e figures show that the number of larger
villages h a s increased in t h e most marked m a n n e r a t the expense of t h e smaller ones in each division of the Province. But in the
absence of any indication of what is meant by the " village " of the tables of 1868, it is impossible to draw any trustworthy conclusion from the figures. In 1S68 as many as 35.740 villages

LChap. III.

FLOCTUATIONS OF POPULATION

Part II.—Migrations of the People,
thousands across the border of neighbouring districts, and reduces the indigenous proportion of
females below that of males, more especially in the Jamna tract. The river which separates us from
the North-West Provinces presents no formidable obstacle to such migration, and the movement
of population across the border is considerable. But the North-West Provinces have also sent us a very
considerable number of immigrants who have accompanied our troops as camp-followers to the furthest
limits of the Province,'and have there settled down as the well-known Purbia population of our cantonment bazaars.
i74- Thus the Panjdb, fast developing under strong and settled rule, has attracted to itself population
from the countries that surround it on all four sides. To the inhabitants of the crowded districts of the Ganges
Do£b it has offered land no less fertile than their own, and more plentiful in proportion to the people to be
fed. To the people of Rajputana it has held out the attractions of a higher rainfall and more ample and easy
irrigation. The wild tribes of the frontier have found in the Indus Valley pastures where they and their herds
are secure from attack; while the people of Kashmir have sought in British territory that help in time of
need which was denied them by their own Government. To the north and west the movement has
been almost wholly in one direction ; but on our eastern and southern borders the immigrants have retained
their connection with their original homes, and more especially have looked for wives for their sons and
husbands for their daughters from among their fathers' people, and a considerable reflex movement has
resulted.
175. The only portion of the Province where real pressure of population is felt is that which includes or
lies immediately under the lower hills, and there the denudation of the hill sides and the constantly increasing damage done by the hill-torrents are yearly making the pressure more and more severe. The parallel zone to the south of it, which combines a fertile soil with facilities for irrigation in perhaps
a higher degree than any other part of the Panjab, has hitherto received the surplus population, while the
construction of the Bari Doab Canal and the Firozpur irrigation works have greatly facilitated the transfer.
And now that the capacity of that fertile zone to receive the surplus numbers of other parts has been taxed
to the utmost, and it possesses as dense a population as it is able to support, the Sarhind Canal is about
to irrigate the central plains, and so to open a wide outlet by which the pressure of population to their north
may find relief. Further to the west the projected canal from the Chanab into the Gujranw^la bar will
perform a similar office for the sub-montane districts of that part of our border; and when these two works
are complete, all fear of over-crowding which cannot be relieved by migration to that moderate distance
which alone the Panjab peasant cares to undertake, will be removed at least for many years. Meanwhile
the people are steadily moving to the large cities in ever increasing numbers, while the villagers are slowly
spreading their habitations over the fields which it is their task to cultivate, and thus the conditions of both
urban and rural life are tending, very slowly indeed, to approach more nearly to those which obtain in England.
The development of the Province under British rule and the peace and order which have accompanied it have
rendered possible the movements I have described. The facilities now afforded for safe and easy locomotion enable surplus hands to leave the over-crowded rural tracts for the centres of commerce or the sites of
large engineering works; while the settler in a strange country is now secure of his life and property.
Above all the great irrigation works executed by us have extended the area and raised the standard of
cultivation in the great plains of the Province ; our railways, by connecting them with the markets of Europe, have raised the demand for their produce ; and thus have been afForded certain means of subsistence to the increasing population which under our rule is no longer wasted by war or decimated by famine.

BANNU—Has a very_ large immigration from Afghanistan, partly due to the bad seasons preceding- the Census which
drove the frontier tribes into our territory in search of labour, but more largely to periodic migration, arid still more so to
the permanent settling of these men in lands acquired by them on the border of the district, a process which has gone
on in Bannu and Peshawar probably to a larger extent than in any other frontier district. The moderate percentage of males shows that no very large proportion of the immigrants consists of labourers in
search of work. Deducting this migration, movement to and from the district is pretty evenly balanced, and is not extensive, being largest in the case of Derah Ismail Khan, to which Bannu had sent, at the
time of the Census, a considerable number of herdsmen from the Mianwali steppes in search of pasture in the wide Indus Valley of the former district.

PESHAWAR.—The figures bear on their face marks of the attraction exercised by a large military and commercial
centre, and of the extraordinary demand for labour that existed at the time of the Census o\\'u\% to the Kabul campaign,
and the Railway and Swat canal works. Immigrants are more than six times as numerous as emigrants, and the
exceedingly high proportion of males among the former show how largely temporary the immigration was. Nearly
half the immigration was from Afghanistan; and here the more moderate percentage of males shows that much of
the movement is due to the settlement of border tribes just described under the Bannu district, and to the periodic
migration alluded to In section 142. The immigration from the North-West Province^ is in connection with the troops,
that from Europe consists of course of the troops themselves, while that from Kashmir consists of famine fugitives in
search of labour. Excepting these countries, trie immigration into Peshawar, though varied, is not extensive in any
single case. The emigration is inconsiderable save to the Railway and road works of Rawalpindi and Kohat; and
to Hazara, probably in search of pasture.

FLUCTUATIONS OF POPULATION.

Part III.—Increase and Decrease of Population.

PART III.-INCREASE AND DECREASE OF POPULATION.
176. Tables and figures.— No reliable statistics of the population of Native States being in existence of ;i dal.p prior to
the present Census, this portion of tbe Chapter deals only with British Territory, and has no concern cither with Native Status
or with the Province as a. whole. The statistics of increase and decrease are contained in Tables I t and XIX, Appendix A,
the former of which refers to districts, while the latter gives details for individual towns. Tbe comparison is, of course, based
upon the figures of 1855 and 1868, the accuracy of which is discussed in. section 178. Supplementary Tables J and K oE Appendix C give the estimated population of each district for each year from 1882 to 1891 assuming post rates of increase ta continue
unaltered, and the population of each Municipality according to the three enumerations of 1868, 1875, and 1881. But before U10
figures of past years could he utilised for tbe purpose of comparison, it was necessary as far as possible to correct them so as to allow
for alterations of boundary which have taken place. So far as tbe figures of 1855 are concerned, any such correction was wholly out
of the question. The boundaries of the Province, including the Dehli Territory, have changed considerably since that year,
while its internal division into districts has been altogether recast. Thus all that can be done is to mate such use as is possible
of the figures as they stand, hearing in mind the changes that have taken place.
Since 1868, however, the alterations in the boundaries of British Territory as a whole have been very small, being wholly due to
river action. But on examining tbe figures of 1S68, it

North-West frontier was not precisely the same as that to which tbe present operations extended. The Deputy Commissioner of Peshawar then wrote: "The area of the district has been taken up to the red line which marks an imaginary boundary between British
" and Independent Territory; but the real limits of the Census are well within this line ;" and evcu in 18S1 the Commissioner of
Peshawar was called upon for a ruling as to whether certain villages were or were not to be considered as belonging to the

in this direction, If any, they are certainly very small, and probably include tracts which were excluded from the former Census.
177. Within the Province transfers of territory from one district to another have been numerous, and in some cases very extensive.
I attempted in the first instance to base the neeessary corrections upon the detailed registers showing the population of each village
which had been prepared at the last Census. But in many districts these figures did not agree with those of the printed tables, and
in some cases the discrepancies were enormous. Thus in Jalandhar the registers showed 40,000 too few males and 19,000 too many
females, while in both Jhang and Rawalpindi the difference exceeded 6,000 souls, and no examination of the figures threw any light ou
the matter 1 . This attempt therefore had to be abandoned, and I was compelled to make the adjustments by taking the printed tables as
correctly representing tbe population of tbe several districts as they stood in 1868, and adding or deducting the population of such
villages as were known to have been transferred to or from each since that year. I fear some transfers may have escaped notice ;
but the resulting error, if any, will certainly be insignificant in comparison with the total population of the district concerned. The
figures thus corrected form the basis of Table I I .
In the case of individual towns there was literally nothing on record to tell us what boundaries had been followed in 1868.
"Wherever tbe records of the last Census gave us separate details of population for urban suburbs, I have included the population
of the suburbs now taken as part of the town in tbe figures for 1868 given in Table XIX. Where this was not the case there was
nothing for it but to accept the published figures of 1868 as they stood. In tbe case of Municipal towns we have an intermediate
set of figures available for comparison, as a separate Census of almost all of them was taken on the 28th February 1875- In the
report of"that Census,, indeed, an entirely new set of figures are given for 1868, which agree neither with those of the published
report of that year, nor with the figures now given in Table XIX. I t does not appear how those figures were obtained2. But as
regards the Census of 1875 we know exactly what boundaries were followed, as the Census was, in all cases, of the population living
within municipal limits.
178. Increase due to greater accuracy of enumeration.—The increase or decrease of the population
of a given tract of country during the interval between any two enumerations, as shown by a comparison
of the figures of the one with those of the other, may be due to any combination of the following causes: —
(1) Greater accuracy of enumeration on the one occasion than on the other;
(2) Movement of population into or out of the tract during the interval ;
(3) Actual increase or decrease of resident population owing to the number of births during the
interval having been greater or less than the number of deaths.
And first as to the comparative accuracy of the respective enumerations. It follows almost necessarily from
the very nature of things that in 1868 greater accuracy should have been attained than in 1855, and in
1881 than in 1868. In 1855 the Province had not long come under our rule, while even the last thirteen
years have seen a great improvement in the.administrative machinery, and especially in the revenue staff
upon which so large a part of the operations devolved. The system of the present Census was elaborated
with far greater pains and minuteness, and far more care was taken to secure uniformity and accuracy
than on either of the previous occasions. Above all, whereas at former enumerations a mere figure was
given for the total number of souls dwelling in each house, in the present Census each person was separately entered by name; and it is difficult to overrate the capital importance of this change in securing
accuracy of enumeration. Meanwhile the people, ignorant always, and at first suspicious of any new thing,

have been growing more and more accustomed to statistical inquiry and less and less fearful of the motives
of Government, while the prejudices which are by no means the smallest of the difficulties to be overcome
in an Indian Census have probably weakened in some slight degree. On the frontier especially there has
been less difficulty experienced in this than in the last Census, when the susceptibilities of the people were
more easily aroused and their jealousy and suspicion of our actions greater than now 1 . Thus it may
fairly be assumed that successive enumerations have been marked by increasing accuracy, and the
assumption is supported by a very strong body of testimony from officials, both Native and European, who
took part in the last Census. So too the increase in accuracy has probably been largest in those parts
where an enumeration of the people is most difficult.
Now the faults of a Census enumeration are almost exclusively those of omission. Where, as now, the record is made by name, they are probably entirely so, for it is hardly possible to conceive that imaginary persons
should be entered: where, as formerly, mere numbers are given, there is not so much certainty, for a careless
man is as likely to overstate as to understate the total number of souls in his house. But even there
the number of males, females, children,youths and adults were separately shown, and it is probable thatunless
some special object was to be gained by exaggeration, such errors as may have occurred tended to give too
small rather than too large a population 2 . Thus some part of the increase shown by our figures may be
attributed to greater accuracy of enumeration; and that part is probably least in the Eastern Plains,
somewhat greater in the Western Plains, greater again (still following the order of difficulty) in the hills,
and greatest of all on the frontier.
179. The proportion of the Sexes a test Of accuracy.—It is impossible to estimate the degree in
which increased accuracy may have affected the figures. The percentage of increase clue to this cause is
probably, in most districts at least, exceedingly small. But there is one test which we can apply, which
• will in some degree measure at any rate the relative increase of accuracy: it is the proportion of the
sexes. It is notorious that the prejudices of the Indian people disincline them to state the number
of their women folk, or even to admit their existence ; and no better proof can be adduced of the greater
care with which one enumeration has been effected in comparison with another, or of the greater success
with which it has approximated to the actual facts, than its showing a smaller ratio of "males to total
population. In 1855 the number of males per 10,000 of both sexes was 5,517 and ranged from 5,702 to
5,265 ; in 1868 it had fallen to 5,448, the extreme figures being 5,605 and 5,213 ; it is now 5,416, the variations
lying between 5,584 and 5,211, and this notwithstanding the fact that special circumstances had induced a
large temporary influx of male immigrants at the time of the late Census.
180. Abstract No. 38 on the opposite page compares the proportion of males to persons for the three
enumerations in each district, the districts being arranged in order of magnitude of the proportion of males
at the Census of 1855. If it is true that the high percentage of males is due in large part to defects of
enumeration, that each enumeration is more accurate than the preceding one, and that the increase in
accuracy is greatest where the former defects were most marked, we shall expect to find, first that the
percentage of males has decreased in every district at each enumeration, or in other words, that all the
figures of columns 6 to 8 of the abstract are positive ; and secondly that, broadly speaking, thai decrease is
greatest where the percentage of males was formerly highest—in other words, that the serial numbers in
columns 9 to 11 and again in columns 12 and 13 correspond.
With.regard to the first test it will be noticed that out of the 31 districts (omitting Simla), the percentage of males is lower in 1881 than it was in 1855 in all but three districts, lower in 1 86S than in 1855
in all but five districts, and lower in 1881 than in 1868 in all but nine districts ; while most of the exceptions
are at once accounted for by the enormous number of coolies and labourers temporarily collected at the
time of the Census in the Rawalpindi and Peshdwar divisions. As for the second test, it cannot of course
be expected that the districts will stand exactly in the order which they should theoretically occupy. The
circumstances of each—indeed the very boundaries of each—vary from Census to Census, for the figures
apply to the districts as they stood at the time in each ease ; the numbers concerned are often small; and
all that can be looked for is a general correspondence in those districts in which no special circumstances
exist to affect the figures. Now a general correspondence does exist between the series in columns g, 10,
and 11, and again between those in columns 12 and 13; that is to say, the districts that are respectively high

181. Discrimination of that portion of t h e increase due to migration.—A far more important (arror
in the increase and decrease of numbers is the actual movement of population from one place to anoiluT.
Unfortunately it is almost impossible to separate this clement from the normal increase due to cxci.;ss o\
births over deaths. Our figures for increase refer to the fixed period of time between two CTuimcraiion^,
whereas our figures for migration include the whole lifetime of the present generation. Of ilirce men
born in Kashmir, one of whom emigrated to the Panjab in 1S54, another in 1S67, and the third in iSSo. all
three will be shq,\vn as immigrants in the migration tigures, but the figures for increase between iSbS and
i88i will include one, and those between 1855 and i8Si two of them only. Moreo\er the j.iresent tigurvinclude the children of immigrants who have come into the tract since t!ie_ ]ire\"ious enumeration, ani.i who
are therefore not represented in the initial population on which the increase is reckoned- On thr otlur
hand the migration ligures do not represent the whole of the movement which affects the increase; and
this imperfection acts in either of two directions, according as the ligures lor migration oinii. to takr
account of movements which have resulted in increase and decrease, or show movements which have had
no such result. For instance, in 1868 there must have biH'^n a largt: number of labourers at work on tli-^
railway Hne between Jagadhri and Jillandhar, man)- of whom had been attracted from other districts, and
thus helped to swell the population, as shown by the enumeration ol that year, of the tract in which ihcv
were working, and to diminish that of the tract from which thev hail come. Hut when the work was o\ er i!n- •
greater number of them probably returned to their homes, and thus they do not apprar at all in \\-\c presrni
ligures for migration, though the fact that thev \\'ere enumerated in one place in tS6S and in an.nluT in
iSSl causes an apparent decrease in tlie population of the former and increase in that of the lalter tract,
which is wholly due to movement of population. Exactly the opposite result occurs in the case of mo>t

Part III.—Increase and Decrease of Population.
Pan jab of 17,824 souls ; and as there is practically no emigration proper from the Panjab to Europe, the
whole of this movement is rightly shown as gain' by migration. But although it is probable that by far
the greater number of these 17,824 persons have entered the Panjab since 1855, yet it is also probable
that in 1855 there were very nearly as many Europeans in the Province, who have since then returned to
Europe, their place being taken by the new comers ; and thus the immigration, while it represents actual gain
to the Panjab population, does not represent increase since 1855, although the individual immigrants have
entered the Province since that year. At a future Census a comparison of the birth-place figures as they
then stand with those of the present Census will render possible an estimate of the amount of migration
which has taken place within the interval. But no record of birth-place was made at either of the two
previous enumerations, and any such comparison is in the present case impossible.
182. The problem with which we have to deal may be thus stated. We know that, within the lifetime of
the present generation, the population ot a given tract has increased oy a certain percentage as the result of
mi oration : we know that it has increased during the interval since a previous Census by a certain other percentage: find how much of the former increase is included in the latter, and deducting that portion, how much
of the latter remains as the effect of the natural excess of births over deaths. Had we really accurate, or
even approximately accurate statistics of births and deaths, the solution would be simple enough. But
this is far from being the case. We have only just begun to register births outside the large towns ; there
is reason to believe that the urban and rural rates differ enormously ; and a glance at Supplementary Table
L of Appendix C, which gives death-rates as registered for the last 12 years, is sufficient to show
how incomplete the registration must be in many of the Panjab districts. Great advances have been
made ; but it will be long before we are able to construct really trustworthy life-tables for the Panjab.
In the absence of such tables there are three points of view from which our problem may be attacked,
all of them uncertain iiwtheir application.
Where the conditions which determine the natural increase of population are identical in any two tracts,
but the rate of increase since last Census has been greater in the one than the other, it follows that
the gain by migration since last Census has been greater in the former than in the latter. Suppose two
districts, each with a population of 4,000 souls in 1868, and in each of which the total gain by migration has
been 3,000, but the present populations of which are respectively 5,000 and 6,000 : if the normal rate
of increase is identical in both, it follows that, even supposing the whole gain by migration in the former
district to have taken place before 1868, at least 1,000 of the similar gain to the latter district must be
of a date subsequent to that year.
The second test is based upon the assumption that the rate of natural increase is tolerably
constant in the same district. If it were quite constant, the population of 1881 would bear the same
proportion to that of 1868 as that of 1868 did to that of 1855,—excluding migration from consideration—
since the'two intervals between the successive enumerations are equal; and if we found that the population of a district was 4,000 in 1855, 6,000 in 1868, and only 8,000 (instead of 9,000) in 1881, we should
conclude that there had been greater gain (or less loss) by migration during the former than during the
latter interval.
The third test is afforded by the proportion between the sexes. . If the gain by migration always
consisted of males and females in the same proportion as the sexes bear to each other in the indigenous
population, the application of this standard would not help us. But this is seldom the case, for, as we
have already seen, either males or females generally predominate among the migrants. Now under norma!
conditions the natural rate of increase by excess of births over deaths will probably be very nearly the
same for both sexes in any given tract. Thus where we find that the increase within a given interval Iras
been markedly greater for one sex than for the other, we may suspect that the tract has gained by migration during that interval if the sex which has increased fastest preponderates among the migrants, or lost
if that sex is in the: minority.
183. Examination of the figures—All three tests are exceedingly difficult of application, and exceedingly uncertain in their indications. We know next to nothing of the vital statistics of the Province
except that they vary enormously, not only from district to district-but from year to year, and that we are
almost wholly ignorant of the conditions which determine their variation. T have already pointed out in
section 131 how delicately poised is the balance between life and death for the great mass of the population,
how little will cause it to incline in one direction or the other, and how violent are the oscillations of the
vital index which result. It is not safe to assume that the natural rate of increase is the same for two contiguous districts with apparently identical physical conformation, for permanent physical conditions are not
perhaps even the most important of the factors concerned. A heavy assessment, a local failure of rain, anyone of a thousand incidental circumstances may disturb the apparent equality. Still less is it possible to
assume that the rate of increase of one period of 13 years is the same as that of the next 13 years, for we
know the exact contrary to be the case. And though we know in general terms the distribution of the
sexes in migration, yet our figures only represent a portion of the actual movement of population, while
increasing accuracy of enumeration ever tends to raise the proportion of females throughout the Province.
Still, a careful examination of the figures in the light of the preceding paragraphs will afford in most
cases a basis for an approximate estimate of the degrees in which increase or decrease is respective!}- due to
migration and to the relative numbers of births and deaths. Such figures as are available are given in
Abstract No. 39 on the opposite page. Unfortunately the boundaries of many of the districts have changed
so entirely since 1855 that no comparison with the figures of that year is possible. Columns 3, 6, and cj
show the net gain by migration, columns 4, 7, and 10 show the increase of population since 1855, a n ^
columns 5, 8, and 11 that since 1868, all in rates per millc of the present population. Columns 12 to 14
show the natural increase since 1855, on the assumption thai all the migration has taken place since
that year. Columns 15 to 17 give similar figures for 186S.

Chap. III. J

FLUCTUATIONS OF

POPULATION.

Part III.=—Increase and Decrease of Population.
Unfortunately the boundaries of some of the districts have changed so much that I have been unable to
give separate figures for them. Even as it is, the respective figures do not in all cases refer to exactly the
same areas; but the difference is generally small. The districts of Hissar and Sirsa, the extraordinary
development of which has so often been alluded to, head the list, the increase since 1855 having been 47 per
cent, in the one and 39 per cent, in the other. In company with them stand the frontier districts of Kohat,
Hazara, and Derah Ghazi, and the dry and healthy districts of Jhang and Rawalpindi. The increase in
the frontier districts is doubtless due in part to more accurate enumeration 1 , and it is probable that Derah
Ismail and Bannu would stand with them if their figures could be separated from those of the canal-irrigated
tracts of Muzaffargarh. Montgomery, Peshawar, and Multan, with their copious irrigation from canals, come
well at the bottom of the districts of the Western Plains, and this notwithstanding that gain by migration
has been greater in the two last than in almost any other of the western districts. The difference between the rates 'of increase in the east and west of the Province respectively is very striking. The
Rawalpindi, Multan, and Derajat divisions taken together have increased by 21 per cent, since 1855, while
the increase in the Dehli and Ambala divisions has been only 7^ per cent. ; and the contrast is chiefly
due to actual difference in the normal rates of increase of the two tracts, for the whole gain by migration
in the western divisions has been only about 5 per cent. But the reason is obvious. In 1855 the
Eastern Panjab had been for 52 years under a strong and orderly rule, while the western districts had only
been six years in our hands.
187. The figures are too incomplete to call for more minute examination; but columns 6 and 7 deserve
a word of notice. The intervals between the successive enumerations having been identical, the figures of
these columns should be equal; and where they are not equal it follows that the rate of increase during the
last 13 years has been. different from that obtaining during the 13 years previous to 1868. The increase
between 1868 and 1881, however, is smaller than that between 1855 a n d 1881 in every case except in
Montgomery and Multan, where the.increase during the latter interval has been considerably greater than
during the former. The exception is of course due to the extension of canal irrigation which has lately
taken place in those two districts. The generally smaller increase has already been explained by the
famine and disease which succeeded the Census of 1868 and preceded that of 1881. But the cases in
which the contrast is very large are interesting. In Hissar the tide of immigration had evidently ceased
to flow by 1868, while in Sirsa it has continued in almost unabated fulness. The loss to Jhang by emigration to the new canals of the neighbouring districts, most of which are of later date than 1868, accounts
for the contrast between the figures. The emigration from the crowded districts of the Jalandhar and
Amritsar divisions, also, has evidently largely taken place within the last 13 years, the rate of increase in
these districts between 1855 and 1868 having been quite normal.
188. Increase since 1868, W e s t e r n Districts.—Abstract No. 42 on the opposite page gives statistics
regarding the increase of population since 1868 2. I have taken the increase in the male population only
for the basis of the abstract, as giving on the whole a more trustworthy indication of real increase as
distinguished from apparent increase due to more accurate enumeration.
The same general features which have already been discussed here present themselves again. The increase altogether has been small owing to the famine and disease which have marked so many of the last
13 years. But these influences have had much less effect in the western than in the eastern districts. Not
only are the former with their small rainfall generally far healthier than the latter, but their cultivation is
almost entirely protected by irrigation, and failure of rain means only a smaller yield, whereas in the east it
means that no crops are even sown over a large proportion of the area. Moreover, as Mr. Dames remarks
of Derah Ismail Khan—
" B a d seasons and h i g h prices do n o t operate w i t h tho same force on a scattered population accustomed to regard bad seasons
" as a p a r t of. t h e order of nature, a n d n o t as abnormal visitations, as they do in t h e more favoured parts of I n d i a where the conditions
" of life allow t h e -population t o increase up to the verge of subsistence, and where a failure of crops means famine. The famine
" prices of B e h a r a n d O u d h would here b e considered as phjenomenally low, y e t t h e prevailing h i g h prices do n o t betoken aiiylc
t h i n g resembling famine, and have no effect in checking the n a t u r a l expansion of the population."

Especially the increase lias been large in the frontier districts, partly because of special circumstances
which created a temporary demand for labour, but still more because in those districts peace and order have
made greater advances within the last 13 years than in any other part of the Province. Major Plowden
writes from Kohat:—•
" I t is a common s a y i n g i n those villages more exposed t h a u others t o incursions from trans-border, t h a t whereas formerly t h e y
" could only cultivate w i t h i n g u n s h o t of t h e i r villages, they can now do so wherever water will reach."

With them stand at the top of the list the not long ago desert district of Sirsa 3 and the districts of Firozpur, Lahore, Multan, and Montgomery, in which canal irrigation has been enormously extended since 1868.
In all these districts the increase lies between \%\ and 16 per cent., or, taking both sexes into account,
between 20 and 13 per cent. Considering the immigration into Muzaffargarh, almost all of which is of
recent date, the low rate of increase is extraordinary, and seems to point to the same unhealthiness and
infecundity as results of extensive canal irrigation of which I shall presently display more lamentable examples in the Dehli Division. Emigration to the new canals explains the small increase in Jhang, Shahpur,
and Gujranwala; the population of Derah Ismail is uncertain, depending much upon the amount of pawindah immigration for each year; while some cause or other, probably pressure of population, is driving
people out of Gujrat; and this brings us to the second break in the figures of column 3, the increase in the
districts mentioned above lying between 13 and 9 per cent., or, if both sexes be taken, between 14 and
12 per cent. Here the average for British Territory divides the list into two parts, and also sepa1
It is just possible that the feudal territories of Tanawal and Teri in Hazara and Kohat respectively were not included in the
Census of 1855.
- I should like to have compared this increase with increase in cultivation during the same period. But the available figures
for cultivation are so absolutely worthless (showing, for instance, that t h e cultivated area in the Montgomery district has decreased
b y 33 per cent, since 1868) that I will not waste time over them.
3
It is worthy of note that Sirsa is now making up its proportion of females, which is always low in an immigrant population
attracted to a developing district. T h e increase in females has been 22 per cent, and in males only i 8 i per cent.

Part III.—Increase and Decrease of Population.
continuous swamps have poisoned the air with miasma, killing or enfeebling the people, and rendering the
men impotent and the women barren. So long ago as 1856 the officer sent by Government to report on
the tract spoke of " the spectacle of sick women and diseased children crouching among the ruins of their
houses (for in many cases the very rafters had been sold), of haggard cultivators wading in the swamps and
watching their sickly crops, or attempting to pasture their bony cattle on the unwholesome grass." For
40 years this evil has been permitted to continue, and now it is to be hoped that the new works at last
nearing completion will do much to remedy it. In the 19 villages of the Karnal district which had
suffered most severely from drought in 1877, the population was found to have decreased between 1868
and 1881 from 37,202 to 30,759. But here the decrease was only temporary. The land was still there,
the people were still alive in some neighbouring tract where they had found employment for a while, and at
the present time at which 1 write they have probably returned to their homes and resumed the cultivation
of their fields. In the 20 villages of the same district which had suffered most severely from the canal,
the population was said to have decreased between 1868 and 1881 from 54,791 to 44,561. But here the
decrease was permanent. The parents had died untimely, the children who should have taken their
place had never been born, while those who had left the home of their fathers in search of new land will
never return to the acres of snow-white salt which now represent what was once a smiling sheet of
cultivation. In the Kaithal tahsil, where the famine of 1868-69 was officially declared to have been
more severe than in any other part of the Province, the population has increased by 6 per cent. In the
Karnal and Panipat tahsils, which are "protected" by the Western Jamna Canal, it has fallen off by 2$
percent. In Dehli the evil is no less marked. The population of Balabgarh, where there is no canal,
shows an increase of 9 per cent., while that of the canal-watered tract of Sunpat has decreased by 4 per
cent. Out of 22 selected canal villages the decrease is 38 per cent, in 1, over 30 per cent, in 4, over
25 per cent, in 8, and over 15 per cent, in 15 ; while 10 per cent, is the smallest decrease, and the total
population has fallen from 25,381 to 19,365 since 1868. In 1877 a special Census was taken of 25 canal
villages in tahsil Sunpat, and taking their population in 1868 as 100, it had decreased to 95-6 in 1877
and to 92-5 in 1881. In 1880, a healthy year, the birth-rate for the Dehli Canal villages was 31 and
the death-rate 47 ; in 1879, a year of fever, the corresponding rates were 24 and 65, and in the canal
villages of Karnal 22 and 76.
190. In the remaining districts of the Panjab there has been an actual decrease of population since
1868; and, with the two exceptions of Kangra and Gurgaon to be referred to presently, they are all
sub-montane districts. Here too disease has made terrible havoc within the last few years. But this is not
the main cause of the decrease. The districts are distinctly over-populated ; the denudation of the lower
hills has not only deprived a considerable portion of the population of the subsistence they derived from
• pasturing their flocks and collecting wood and other forest produce in the minor ranges, but has resulted
in actual destruction of cultivation by the hill torrents'as they flow through the fertile plains below. Thus
emigration has been extensive, while the railway has drawn away their urban population, and the rapidly
developing districts which lie below them have profited by both movements. In Kangra the same causes
have been at work to some extent, as the population is very large in proportion to the culturable area. But I
believe that the apparent decrease is due in large part to an error in the figures of the last Census. The details now existing in the district office fall short of the published totals by several thousands, and I cannot help
thinking that they are right and the totals wrong. Moreover, it is stated that at the Census of 186S no precautions were taken against double enumeration in Spitiand Lahul,and that when these tracts were censused after
the opening of the passes, a considerable population was counted over .again who had already been enumerated during the winter months in the lower valleys of Kulu and Kangra, In Gurgaem very special causes have
contributed to cause the decrease. In the first place this district bore the full brunt of that terrible scourge
of fever which in 1878-79 literally decimated the population of some of the western districts of the NorthWest Provinces, but which was felt only in diminished intensity to the west of Dehli. The figures are given
in Supplementary Table L, Appendix C. It must be remembered "that it is fever, not cholera, that kills our
Panjabis, as a reference to Abstract No. 21 on page 56 will show. Between 1868 and 1S81 about six million
deaths were registered in the Panjdb, of which four millions were ascribed to fever and only 100,000 to
cholera. The intimate connection between the amount of rainfall and the number of deaths by fever has
been elaborately discussed by Dr. Bellew in the Sanitary Report of 1880. Rain produces chill, and chill
fever; and hence arises the great superiority in the matter of healthiness of our western over cur eastern
districts. In the month of October 1879 the death-rates per mille per annum
from fever alone reached the terrible figures shown in the margin. Further, it
so happened that just as disease and drought were trying the people of Gurgaon

192. Future increase and decrease of population.—Hitherto all sanitary and other statistics have
been calculated on the figures of the Census of 1868 ; for the changes in boundaries between that Census and
the enumeration of 1855 were too great to allow of any detailed comparison of the two sets of figures. We
are now, however, able to state the rate of increase and decrease of population for each district and division
during the last 13 years; and I have accordingly given in Supplementary Table J, Appendix C, the
population of each district for each year from 1882 to 1891 inclusive, supposing- the rate of increase and
decrease which obtained between 1868 and 1881 to continue. It is probable that the rate of increase will
diminish in those districts which have been gaining most by immigration ; and especially in those, such as
Kohi.t, Jahlam, Peshawar, and Rawalpindi, in which the immigration was largely due to exceptional and
temporary conditions. And it is to be hoped that the rate of increase will grow higher in the districts of
the Dehli division and in Rohtak, where the unusual mortality of late years has diminished it. But in the
case of the remaining districts at any rate, I believe that the figures of this table will give a more trustworthy basis for vital statistics than can be obtained by taking the figures of the present Census unaltered for the next ten years.
