I now t u r n to the eight district officers who are less positive as to the non-existence of infanticide.
Captain Bartholomew of J h a n g writes : " Girls are not actually ill-treated; b u t their birth is often con" sidered a misfortune, a n d it is easy to u n d e r s t a n d how neglect without actual ill-usage increases the
" death-rate/'
In Gurd^spur infanticide is said to be practised " if at all, only among the Bedi K h a t r i s . "
Colonel Gurdon of J i l a n d h a r thinks that there is " only neglect, not m u r d e r ; and even t h a t only a m o n g
" high class R a j p u t s or Jats. " T h e D e p u t y Commissioner of Hiss£r explains t h a t although men are often
unable to marry because girls are so expensive, yet girls are not taken so much care of as boys, especially
among Rajputs who give large dowers a n d think it shameful to sell their daughters. Mr. Smyth is of
opinion t h a t there is now no infanticide in the Dehli district, b u t t h a t Hindus t r e a t their girls carelessly
while Musalmans do n o t ; y e t the Hindus and Hindu converts pay for their brides, while the foreign
Mahomedans do not. Mr. Benton of Karndl writes, apparently more from the result of an examination of
the figures than from personal knowledge : —
" There is no doubt that infanticide, if not general, still exists among the agricultural population to a much larger extent
" than could have been imagined. There are strong motives for getting rid of a superabundant family of daughters. Although
" in most castes a price can be got for a bride, still where the price is highest the up-bringing of daughters must be a considerable
" loss looking at the matter as one of pure profit and loss ; and to men of respectability who wish to marry their daughters in ac" cordanoe with the prevailing customs, a large family of daughters is universally declared to be a ruinous misfortune.
" I t is admitted on all hands that there is a difference between the treatment of male and female children, but it is not
"admitted that this difference is of a character to cause the destruction of the latter. The total, effect however of a prevailing
" feeling more favourable to males than females may not be inconsiderable, even if it does not go the length of criminality."
Colonel Jenkins writes from K i n g r a : —
" There is a widely prevalent custom, particularly among the Bra"hmarjs and Rajputs, according t o which a man must always
" take a wife from a lower and give his daughter to a higher caste. There is the greatest difference between giving a girl and taking
" a girl. If a Ra*jptit is asked with what class he may intermarry he will usually mention some below his own, but if asked whether
" he would give his daughters to the same tribe in exchauge, would be horrified at the idea. The same rule prevails among the local
*' Brihmans though to a less extent. The result of"this is that it becomes most difficult to obtain a suitable match for high-born girls,
" and there can be no doubt I think that the custom of infanticide is by no means extinct. I t is however practised in a much more
" scientific method than in former days. I t was not long ago that a case of this kind was brought before me in which there was
*' evidence to show that the woman' had deliberately prepared to put an end to the child's life if it should turn out to be a girl, as it
"actually did. She described how a female relative of her's had advised her t o starve the child, roll over it, fling it about, and if
" these methods had not the desired result, give it some opium. I n this case she happened to be discovered, but it is most probable
" that there are many such cases which elude detection. The system adopted for prevention of the crime can only operate as a
" partial check, as the families in which it is most usually committed are more or less influential."
T h e following extract from Mr. Lyall's K ^ n g r a R e p o r t defines the limits and extent of the custom to
which Colonel Jenkins alludes : —
" Except among first-class or Jaika*ri Rajptits and Nagarbotia Br^hmans, (batta-satta ' or exchange betrothals are very coiu" mon, and something is nearly always given as a consideration for the bride. On the other hand, Ra*jputs of high family are heavily
" bribed to marry, owing to the feeling of pride which forbids a Rajput to m a n y a daughter to any but a man of equal or rather
"superior family to his own. The prevention of infanticide, both in our territories and Jammu (where they used to marry many of
" their daughters) now-a-days drives these Ra*jpiits to great straits. Not long ago a Manila's Rajput, who had three daughters, not
" finding any son-in-law of sufficient rank according to his notions, kept them all at home till they were quite old maids. He at
" last found an old bridegroom of ninety, who married two of the three at once for a consideration, but died on the return journey
" home, so that the two brides came back upon their father's hands. Shortly after the third daughter ran away with a post man or
" letter-carrier."
Finally M r . Coldstream, Deputy Commissioner of Hushy£rpur, -who has examined the whole subject
at much length and with g r e a t ability and completeness writes as follows : —
" T h i s difficulty of marrying daughters suitably has operated in past generations, probably for many hundreds of years, to
" foster the barbarous custom of infanticide. Forty years ago probably many hundreds of female children were annually buried in this
" district immediately after birth. When several female children were born in succession the destruction of the last horn was carried
" out with the following observance—a piece of gur was placed in the mouth of the child, a skein of eottou was laid on her breast,
" and the following incantation recited two or three times :—
* Eat gur, spin your thread,
We don't want you, but a brother instead.'
"Theiufants were usually put into gharras or water-pots and buried in the ground. Sometimes a Brahman or ilahajan
" would be on the outlook, and rescue the child and bring it up as an adopted daughter. To such an act much religious merit was
" supposed t o attach. Several living memorials, women who had in infancy been so rescued, are alive, or were till lately, in this
"district. I n the Police division of Hajfpur in 1867 the following statistics were collected. In 36 villages consisting of 1,013
" houses of Rajputs of all denominations, there were found to have died 10 per cent, within the year. Among other tribes about
" 5 per cent, only had died. The Report which was then drawn up by the Inspector of Police, Mir Fazl Husen, states ' the parents
" ' have hundreds of ways at their command to put a female child to death, and can defy all the efforts of the Police to detect them.
" ' T h e plan which the parents now adopt is to report sickness, and then death, which is sure to follow. Their Hakims refuse to give
"'medicines because they know it will never be given, and that the application to them was nothing more nor less than a blind to
" * be used if occasion should arise. They are heartlessly careless of their daughters' health : they expose them to all the inclemencies
" ' of the weather, and sometimes buy strong medicines to try to bring on sickness: the mother even sometimes causing her infant
" ' daughter to refuse her natural nourishment by rubbing the nipple over with bitter aloes and other specifics.'
" At the time.of preparation of this report Mr. Perkins, Deputy Commissioner, prepared a statement which showed in mimer" ous-villages an abnormal and significant disproportion in the number of girls in Hajput families. The boys alive were in number
" 1,74.8: the girls alive were only 944. As I have not received back the village schedules from the Census office, I am not in a po»i" tion to make an exact comparison ; but I may say that I am satisfied from enquiries frequently made that matters are now much
" better, and that female children are now neither ruthlessly destroyed in any appreciable numbers, nor are they so carelessly treated.
" At the same time, while I believe that the crime of female infanticide has to a large extent been banished from the land, I am not at
' " all sure that the small proportion of women is not in part due to a certain popular depreciation of female life common in the country :
" the moral inheritance of past years, the trace of a barbarous sentiment which had for centuries been cherished throughout North
" I n d i a . I can imagine that this estimate of female life works almost unconsciously in the minds of the people, and that while most
" parents would hardly own it to themselves, it is very probable that among certain sections of the population daughters are less
" carefully nourished and protected through the helplessness of early infancy and the dangers of later childhood.
" T h e Naib Tabsildar of the sub-division of Arab where Rajputs most abound, who has been there six years and knows the
" people well, says that there is no female infanticide among the Rajputs. And in the Unah tahsil where there are most Rajput^
" ( t h e class which was in older times most given to the barbarous practico), it is satisfactory to observe that the female population is
" above the average, vie,r 47 per cent. This result may be held to justify the action lately taken by Government in withdrawing the

" J am glad here to be able to insert opinions of a number of intelligent men, who have acted as supervising officers in the

"'the props of a family; girls are its weakness,-causing expense and returning no income.'
" As I have remarked above, there is, I think, some, indication given in the statistics of the existence of a certain popular depreciation ofiemale child life."
711. C o n c l u s i o n s a s t o t h e p r e v a l e n c e of infanticide.—This last sentence appears to me exactly to
express the existing state of affairs. That infanticide is practised at all generally I do not believe ; that
it Is habitual with- any class I d o u b t ; and if with any, it is I think only with some exceedingly limited
sections of the community, such as perhaps the Bedi families of Gurdispur, and even there takes the form
of intentional-neglect rather than actual murder. But there is not the slightest doubt that the life of a
girl i s ' l e s s valued and worse cared forthan that of a boy; chiefly indeed among the hypergamous classes
who cannot find husbands for them, the higher castes of the eastern Panjifb who will not sell their
daughters, and the Hindus who spend much money on their marriage and account it shameful to
leave them Unmarried; but also in a less degree and as a relic of the old fighting days, and perhaps from
tfoe contagion of Hindu ideas, among all other classes of the Panjdb people without distinction of race, religion, or locality.

712. Unsatisfactory nature of the figures for occupations.—I have left the consideration of the
statistics for occupations till every other portion of my Report is complete, in the hope that the printed
tables might b e ready in time. But as I take up my pen, with only a few days remaining of the period
allowed for the completion of the Report, and with no other subjects left to be considered, the male tables
are only complete for 12 out of the 32 districts, while the female tables for divisions even are still unfinished
and no part of the occupation tables for Native States is yet in t y p e ; and this though the printing of the
final tables has been going on continuously, and without any delay due to my office, for the last fourteen
months. Even were the copy not in the printer's hands, it would be impossible to work with manuscript
tables so cumbrous and complex as are the occupation tables for the Panjab, and I am therefore compelled to content myself with a general review of the subject, and to omit all reference to the detailed
figures for districts, which indeed are not available for the purpose.
I think on the whole that the figures for occupation a r e the least satisfactory among the results of the
present Census. It is not so much that the original entries in the schedules were actually wrong, indeed
I believe that as far as they went they were very seldom inaccurate ; but that they were very often unnecessarily indefinite and vague in their meaning 1 . A n d such meaning as they had has been obscured
by the adoption of a system of classification so ill adapted to the social ceconomy of t h e Panjab, that I
should be hardly exaggerating were I to say that it has, by the form in which it has presented the results,
very largely destroyed their interest and value. I shall presently explain under what circumstances that
classification was, almost of necessity, adopted. T o obtain figures which should really represent the distribution of the population of the Province by occupation, nothing short of recasting the whole of the tables
would suffice. Thus all that I shall attempt is to explain the actual significance and composition of the
detailed figures in such a manner as will enable any person referring to the tables to extract from them
so far as is possible the information he may require, and to discuss very briefly the general conclusions to
be drawn from the figures. I shall print the general discussion first, and follow it with the detailed explanations in small type as P a r t II of the Chapter.

713. The industrial ceconomy of England and the Panjab.—Much of the confusion of the figures
and of the uncertainty which attaches to their meaning is inherent in the very nature of the subjectmatter. W e have not here in the Panjab, and least of all in the villages of the Panjab, a differentiation
of occupations such as exists in England, where each definite craft or minute branch of labour is confined
to a specific class of workmen who follow that craft exclusively. In the towns, where alone are to be
found such of the more delicate and elaborate industries as are practised at all in the Panjab, division of
labour is carried out to a certain extent. But even there the great mass of the artisans work, not in factories or for jcapitalists or large employers of labour, but as private and individual workmen, each man
beginning, carrying on, and completing the articles which he produces. And in the villages the different
crafts are not even followed by separate persons. I have already described in section 62 how all the
rude arts necessary to supply the simple wants of the Panjab villager are carried on within the walls of the
village itself; and I have explained in section 570 how much of the labour is performed by village menials
receiving customary dues and rendering customary services. In such primitive societies, where the community is limited in extent and no demand exists for skilled workmanship, it may be conceived that the
same craftsman commonly follows several callings which in a more advanced and highly organised community would be kept distinct. . I have shown in discussing the menial and artisan castes how impossible
it is to draw any definite lines between the numerous castes whose very basis is the hereditary occupation
they follow, and the same vagueness and uncertainty extends to the callings of the individuals composing those
castes. One man combines weaving with tanning and working in leather and general coolies' work, another
with scavengering and working in grass and straw ; the water-carrier fishes and makes baskets, while his wife
cooks and acts as midwife ; the potter makes bricks and is the carrier of the village ; the carpenter works
in iron and the blacksmith in wood, while both act as bricklayers and stone-masons ; the oil-presser scutches
cotton and slaughters and dresses sheep, and so on throughout the list. And finally every one or almost
every one of them works in the fields either continuously or at certain seasons. In the east of the Panjab
the common custom is for each family of leather-workers to furnish one able-bodied man for continuous
field-work, and two brothers will take it turn about, ploughing one day and making shoes the other. And
the vagueness and indefiniteness which thus characterises the practice of the great mass of the people has
not unnaturally extended to their very conception of occupation. They think that the name of the caste
to which a menial or artisan belongs is a quite sufficiently accurate and comprehensive definition of
his occupation, and that to tell you that a man is a Machhi and his wife a Machhin is to tell you all
that there is to be told, though a Machhi besides working in the fields is a cook, a waterman, a carrier of
burdens and palanquins, a fisherman, a boatman, a maker of baskets, a grain parcher, and a baker, while
his wife often helps him in almost all of these pursuits, and is a midwife to boot. And indeed it not
unfrequently happens that the same man actually follows all or nearly all of these occupations, and that it
is exceedingly difficult to say that he derives his support from any one of them rather than from the r e s t ;
1

return of male occupations is in the case of the Hill States, where it is said that the number of cultivators was purposely returned*both by
officials and by private individuals as much smaller than the reality, for fear on the one hand that the true figures should afford a clue to
the real revenue of the State, and on the other that they should lead to increased taxation.

714. Difficulties of classification.—But when we came to tabulate such entries as Michhi in accordance with a classification of occupations based upon the minute and definite division of labour which
characterises English industries, and especially when a part of that classification was made in ten separate
offices and in accordance with ten separate views of the distinctive occupation of a Mdchhi, it may be
conceived what confusion resulted. My orders to the divisional officers were that they were to take together such entries as conveyed precisely the same meaning though in different language. T h e separate
forms assumed by the entries of occupation must have numbered many thousands, and it would have been
absurd to have tabulated separate figures for hajjam and bd/ katna, for " b a r b e r " and " h a i r - c u t t e r . "
At the same time I directed them in no case to put together any two entries between the meaning of which
any difference at all existed. Unfortunately their views as to identity of meaning, while they differed in
form, agreed in their expansive nature. One man put Chamir and " b o o t - m a k e r " together, another,
Chamir and " t a n n e r ; " one took M^ehhi and " c o o k " as having precisely the same meaning, another
Machhi and " w a t e r - c a r r i e r . " And indeed not only were both right in a sense, but each was probably as
nearly right as was possible for the locality for which he was tabulating the figures ; for the staff was especially selected for local knowledge and experience, and as I have shown elsewhere, not only is the same
word used to denote totally different occupations in different parts of the Province, but the group of occupations which is peculiar to, and still more the particular occupation of that group which is most commonly
and distinctively followed by one and the same caste, varies from one place to another. As it was, the
number of different headings for occupations returned t o my office, after the divisional officers had finished
their classification, was no less than 2,975.
715. Unsuitabtlity of t h e classification a d o p t e d . — T h e fact is that the system of classification was
at fault rather than the method of carrying out that system. The mistake was made of attempting to arrive at a minute detail of distinct occupations which simply has no existence in the practice
of the people. In England not only are the branches into which the various industries are divided much
more numerous than in India, but each is followed by a distinct set of workmen, so that it is possible to
group the figures on an artificial system of classification. In India the same occupations are practised, not
separately but in groups,.and it is impossible to separate them. Yet instead of taking those occupations
together which are practised together, and following the classification on which the whole industrial
ceconomy of the country is based, we attempted to force our material into a form which was not adapted to
it, and spoiled it in the process. W e sifted it with a sieve the meshes of which were too fine to allow the
organic particles of which it is naturally composed to pass, and in forcing it through we broke those
particles and crushed them out of all recognisable shape. The system which compelled the Census Commissioner to class the village Chuhra and Musalli together with beldirs, brick-makers, and lime-burners, as
" w o r k e r s in stone and c l a y " and the village Kahar and Ma'chhi together with icemakers as " w o r k e r s in
w a t e r , " and to put both under the heading " workers and dealers in minerals, " is simply a reductio ad
absurdum of classification.
716. Another difference between the distribution of occupations in India and in England which
caused the adoption of the English classification very seriously to diminish the value of our figures,
has already been alluded to in sections L I , 62. England is essentially a manufacturing and mercantile country. The manufactures are carried on by a separate class, while the collection and distribution
of the products of these industries and the enormous trade of the country are in the hands of a mercantile
community which is exceedingly numerous and important. T h e English classification separates these
great wholesale traders under the head "mercantile," but includes all the small local distributing agency
together with the producers of the articles in which they deal. Thus, while iron merchant is taken
separately, ironmonger is included in the same group with blacksmith. Now the Panjib is neither a
mercantile nor a manufacturing, but an agricultural country'; the great merchants form a very small
portion of the community; and even them it has been impossible to distinguish from the petty dealers
owing to the indefinite nature of the language used, for anaj bechna might mean either a great grain merchant or a small village shop-keeper. So too production and distribution are more often in the hands of
the same person in India than in England. If a villager wants a pot he goes direct to the potter, if a
blanket to the blanket weaver, and not to a shop. On the other hand the petty local distributing agency
which form the great mass of our mercanfV/e classes, occupy by comparison a far more important position
and are possessed of a far more distinctive character in the Panjab than in England. Figures showing
this agency separate from the artisan classes would have possessed great administrative value in the
Panjab. But we were not to have them ; and while our " mercantile " class was left almost blank, " workers
and d e a l e r s " in all sorts of articles and staples were grouped together under the same headings. Nor
did these headings in very many cases adequately represent the commodities dealt in by the persons who
were entered under them, for commerce, like industries, is much less minutely divided in the Panjab than
in England, while the groups of commodities in which the several traders deal respectively differ entirely
from the similar groups into which the petty trade of England divides its staples. Yet another fundamental distinction between the organisation of occupations in the two countries is to be found in the fact
that Government undertakes in India many functions which it leaves to private enterprise in England.
Here it not only concerns itself with administration and defence, but also includes the engineers, the doctors,
the schoolmasters, and a large part of the railway staff of the Province. In short, a system of classification could hardly have been devised more unsuitable to the circumstances of society and the requirements of the administration in the Panjab, or more eminently calculated to produce results which should
neither represent the one nor satisfy the other, than the English system which was followed at the present
Census.
717. Reasons why the English system w a s adopted.—Why then was the English system of classification adopted P In the
first place we bad no other. I t is easy, now that the figures have been tabulated and examined, to pick holes in the classification
followed"; but in the_Panja"b at least we had no material on which to base a more suitable classification.
We know singularly
little of the industrial organisation of the people we govern—less indeed than of their organisation by caste, for the subject hardly
falls within the scope of ordinary official routine. Beyond Mr. Baden-Powell's two valuable volumes on the Products and Manufactures of the Province, Mr. Iloey's Monograph on the Trade and Manufactures of Northern India, and a few scanty notices of
village menials scattered through our Settlement Reports, there is hardly anything in print on Ihe subject; while there is certainly
no officer or group of officers in the Panjab capable of drawing up a scheme of classification which should be even approximately

721. General distribution of male occupations.—Abstract No. 122 on the next cage shows broadly
tlie distribution of male occupations. I have in arranging these figures grouped together as far as was possible those occupations in the separation of which there was most fear of confusion ; for instance I have
included cooks (No. 55 of Tables X I I A and B) with water-carriers (No. 58), since in the centre and west of
the Panjab, where alone the former were returned in any numbers, it was absolutely impossible to separate
the two. T h e detailed remarks on each class which form P a r t II of the present chapter will show under
what explanations and limitations each group of figures must be accepted. But on the whole the grouping
of the Abstract may. I think be taken as representing with considerable accuracy the general distribution by occupation of the male population of over 15 years of age, for it is to it alone that the figures
refer. T h e doubts and uncertainties which attend the minute detail of occupations given in the final tables
still affect in some degree the significance of the figures. But though they cannot be wholly removed, they
do in a great measure disappear in the broader grouping here adopted. Some of them are got rid of by
taking together occupations which the industrial practice of the country renders it impossible to separate
effectually, while still more of them affect small figures only, and are quite unnoticeable when only main
classes are considered. Thus our final tables show 44,963 silversmiths, 111 damasceners, and 70,741 blacksmiths. It is certain that the number of damasceners is understated. But it is equally certain that the
whole number is so small, that whether the missing men have been returned as blacksmiths or silversmiths
they have not appreciably affected the figures.

723. Government Servants.—The group that I have put first consists of all who are in Government
employ, whether concerned in the administration of the country by the various civil departments and the
municipal organisation, or in its defence by the military force. It corresponds with orders 1 and 2 of the
final tables. Of the total numbers included, 48 per cent, are employed in the civil, 16 per cent, in the
municipal and village, and 36 per cent, in the military administration. This group is naturally concentrated to a very large extent in the towns, and is most numerous at the capital of the Province, and where
great cantonments exist. The very large numbers shown for the Rawalpindi and frontier divisions are due
not only to the normal concentration of troops on our frontier, but also to the extraordinary activity in the
Commissariat and Public W o r k s Departments which has already been alluded to as resulting from the
Kabul campaign. T h e class of Government servants is in one respect that section of the community which
is-less than any other affected by distress and famine, for their employment is most permanent in its nature.
On the other hand, their salaries being practically fixed, they feel a rise in prices more severely than the
numerous classes who are either paid in kind, or receive a remuneration which fluctuates with the cost of living
724. Classification of Government Servants.—The classification of persons in Government employ
is one of the most difficult questions connected with statistics of occupations in the Panjab, and, as will
be shown in-Part II of this chapter, the figures are exceedingly unsatisfactory. The functions assumed by
Indian Governments are so diverse, and many of them are so different in their nature from those to which
the English Government confines itself, being connected with the development rather than with the administration or defence of the country, that the same system of classification is not equally suitable to both
countries. Should for instance menials, messengers, and artificers employed in the public offices be
classed as Government servants ? If so, should labourers employed in the excavation of a canal or the
construction of a railway be so classed? If the answer be that the former are permanently and the latter
temporarily employed, how is the line to be drawn in the numerous cases where a permanent subordinate
establishment is temporarily augmented at certain seasons of the year? The primary object of the occupation tables appears to be to inform us by what calling each person earns his living, and not from what
source he receives the wages of that calling ; and I would class all scavengers, porters, blacksmiths, and
other artisans and menials under their proper heads, irrespectively of the question whether they were working
for a Government department or for private employers. So I would not distinguish between schoolmasters
employed by the Educational Department and private schoolmasters, and I would take engineers together
whether they were the servants of a Cpmpany or of Government. The Government can at any moment
obtain full details of its own staff which will be far more accurate and complete than any that a Census
can afford. I would class under Government service only such persons as are actually employed in the
general or local administration, in the assessment and collection of revenue, in the adjudication of disputes,
o r in the detection, prevention, and punishment of crime, or who were attached to the regular forces and
under military discipline. Even then many doubtful cases would arise and would have to be dealt with
separately. For instance, a canal officer is often a revenue collector and a magistrate as much as an engineer. At any rate some definite system should be decided upon before next Census. Owing to the
adoption of the English system in the present Census, we have even in the Imperial tables the telegraph
signallers of the Panjab Northern State Railway classed as "Civil Service" under the head "National
Government," while those of the Sindh, Panjab and Dehli Railway are shown under the sub-order " Messengers and Porters ; " Government hospital assistants are grouped with " National Government," while Government compounders are shown under "physicians, surgeons, and druggists," and so forth; while in the
Provincial tables the classification is even more unsatisfactory, because more uncertain.

727. T e n a n t s . — U n d e r the heading " t e n a n t s " are
included all who take land of a landlord and cultivate it on their own responsibility. In the towns
the tenant class is often of an exceedingly fluctuating
nature, a man seldom holding the same plot for more

the richer lands near the villages in the highly381

THE OCCUPATIONS OF THE PEOPLE.

Part I.—General and Comparative.
cultivated central districts is held on a similar tenure, especially where the owners do not cultivate themselves. In the south-west of the Panjab the tenant is not unfrequently little better than a serf, possessing neither capital nor appliances of his own, and cultivating with his landlord's oxen. But though the
number of tenants who have no certainty of tenure, whether dependent upon law or upon custom, is considerable in itself, it forms but a small fraction of the class as a whole. T h e great mass of the tenants are,
in perhaps most parts of the Panjab, almost as fixed in their holdings for all practical and immediate pur. poses as are the landlords themselves, ejections being exceedingly rare in proportion to the numbers concerned ; while where the tenant is constantly changing the fact is more often due to a competition for labour
than to a scarcity of land, and the tenant abandons his holding, not because the landlord turns him out,
but because he thinks he can obtain better terms elsewhere. Thus so far as the ceconomical distribution
of the population is concerned) the landlords and tenants may almost be taken together, both being d e pendent almost wholly upon the nature of t h e season and the produce of the land, and being little liable
to distress save when these fail them. On the other hand the landlords are, taken as a whole, by far the
wealthier of the two classes, their holdings and their capital are alike larger than those of the tenantry,
their income is, in those parts of the Panjab where true rent exists, supplemented by the rent paid by the
latter, and the margin over and above the bare means of subsistence upon which they can fall back when
distress does arise is larger." And this difference is greatest where the proportion of landlords to tenants is
smallest; in the J a m n a districts, where land-owners ordinarily cultivate themselves, there is often but little to choose between a

728. Agricultural labourers.—The next two groups are headed " j o i n t cultivators" and "agricultural
" labourers." Here I have endeavoured to separate two very distinct classes. The first, known as Sajji,
Adhjogia, or by corresponding terms, is associated with himself by the owner or tenant in the cultivation
of his land, and receives a fixed share of the produce be it great or small. T h e nature of the association
has already been described in section 108 of Chapter II. T h e second class consists of the agricultural
labourers on fixed pay, whether by the day, month, or year. T h e type of the class is the Kamera, Kama, or
Hdli.
But I fear that the two classes have not been carefully distinguished in the schedule entries, and
that a large number of each must have been included in the figures for tenants. According to the figures
- the joint cultivators are less numerous in towns than in villages, and are most common in the east of the
Province ; and this I believe to be in accordance with facts. So too the agricultural labourer is rightly shown
as much more common in the towns than in the villages ; but I believe that the figures under this heading
are much too small for the Western Panjab. According to the Abstract the class is hardly known in the
Multan and Derajat divisions. Both these classes occupy an ceconomical position greatly inferior to that
of t h e t e n a n t ; but of the t w o the joint cultivator has far the more certain means of subsistence. He is,
it is true, no less dependent upon the yield of the harvest than is the owner or tenant himself. But
the partnership is in many cases one of long standing, and cannot at any rate be broken for a year, while
the hopes of the harvest are wholly in the future when the agreement is concluded. The agricultural
labourer on the other hand is at the best only paid by the year, and is often not entertained till the season
has in some measure declared itself; while a large proportion of the class are mere temporary servants
taken on for a short time only when the crops need watching, at harvest, and so forth, and a failure of
rain deprives them of all hopes of employment. T h e y are almost always paid in kind, and are so far independent of a rise in prices.
729. T h e pastoral Class.—The figures for the grazier class are necessarily very imperfect. I have.
as pointed out in Part IT of this chapter, endeavoured in my final tables to separate the cattle-owners
proper, that is those persons who derive their income from the possession of flocks and herds, from those
who merely t e n d cattle. But it is impossible to separate with any completeness the one class from the
other or either from the agriculturists; Every land-owner owns cattle, and as a rule his son tends them.
"Almost every cattle-owner holds land, and as a rule he and his son cultivate it. Still the number of persons returned as owning or tending cattle in the various parts of the Province, though incompletely representing the actual numbers engaged in the occupation, probably gives us a fair idea of the relative decrees
in which pastoral are combined with agricultural pursuits. The number is far highest in the great pasture
lands of the W e s t e r n Plains, while in those alone are people returned as camel and cattle-owners, to the
number of 9,000 in the Multan division and of 1,500 in the Derajat. The detailed figures of the tables
1
The figures are of course based upou the numbers of owners and tenants as shown in the occupation tables, and not upon the
areas cultivated by the two classes respectively.

730. Agriculture combined with Other occupations.—The instructions for filling up the Census
schedules directed that When a person followed two or more occupations, that one only was ordinarily to
b e entered from which he principally derived his living; but that where agriculture was combined with
any other occupation, both were to be shown. T h e rule made a distinction between two similar cases, and
as m i g h t have been expected was very generally neglected. Many of the district officers note that the
figures returned under this heading are absurdly small. It is hardly an exaggeration to say that, at any
r a t e in the eastern half of the Panjab, almost every adult male in a village excepting the shop-keeper does
more or less field-work, and that most adult males who are neither land-owners nor belong to the agricultural menials presently, to b e described cultivate a small plot which they hold either as tenants or on a
grant for service. T h e shop-keeper often owns some of the land of the village, but in the east of the
Province he rarely, if ever, cultivates it himself. In the west however the Aroras are almost as energetic
husbandmen as any other class of the community, while the Census Reports for the districts of the Western
Plains and for Sirsa, where land is plentiful and labour scarce, note almost without exception how
tyniversal is the desire to obtain a piece of land. On the other hand they also notice how strong is the
tendency, so soon as the land is obtained, to give up the hereditary occupation altogether and take to
agriculture o n l y ; and where this has happened the person is rightly entered as a cultivator pure and
simple. T h e omission to record double occupations may take either of two forms. The menial or artisan
Who combines agriculture with his proper handicraft may either enter himself as a cultivator only, or
he may omit all mention of his agricultural occupation and record only his hereditary calling. W h e r e
the omission has taken the latter form it is of small importance, as we know the general facts; but where
it has resulted in a man whose primary occupation is a handicraft being entered as a land-owner or tenant
the error is more material. In the east
menials rarely own land, there being a strong

_ 73?- Village menials.—Thegroup of occupations which comes next in Abstract No. 122, page 380, is that
which includes the village menials. These persons, so far as they are found in villages, and to some extent in

383

™ E OCC^PAT'ONS OF THE PEOPLE,

Part I.—General and Comparative.
towns also, are oeconomically separated from their brother artisans by two very important fails. In the first
place they occupy a recognised position in the village community, performing customary services and receiving in return customary dues which almost invariably take the form of a fixed share of the produce. Thus, with
the exception of the leather-workers who perhaps profit more in seasons of drought by the mortality among
the cattle than they lose by the failure of the crops, they are no less than the agriculturists proper wholly dependent for their support upon the yield of the harvest. In the second place, the first three classes at any rate,
the water-carriers, leather-workers, and scavengers, occupy in the east and centre of the Panj.iba very important position in the agricultural community, much of the hardest field-work being performed by them. In (ailing for Census Reports and indicating the subjects that might profitably be discussed in them, it was particularly requested that Deputy Commissioners would explain the position occupied and duties performed by
village menials in their respective districts. Unfortunately the request has been complied with in veryfew instances, and I therefore treat the subject with great hesitation, though I believe that what 1 am about
to say is generally in accordance with facts. The date fixed for the completion of the Report is so near
that there is no time to obtain information from the districts. Confining then our attention for the present
to the village population, we find that the leather-workers, with whom i have included shoe-makers are
most numerous in the Jamna tracts and the-hills, where they are recognised held labourers and supply a
considerable portion of the agricultural labour employed 1 . In the centre of the Province their place is
taken by the scavengers who there occupy a precisely similar position. So too the watermen, with whom
I have, for reasons given in Part 11 of the Chapter, included those returned as cooks, appear from their
numbers to perform somewhat similar functions in the central districts, though their large number is perhaps
partly due to the custom there prevalent of having public bakeries common to the village. In other parts
of the Province, where scavengers and watermen do not work in the field as part of their ordinary duties,
they are looked upon as luxuries and are chiefly found in villages where tin- women are secluded, where
they are of course a necessity ; and indeed it would appear that in Hushv.lrpur these two classes, and even
the potters also, are often paid fixed wages and not a share of the produce.
733. In the villages of the west of the Panjarj these three classes are returned in strikimdv small
numbers. I think there are several reasons for the difference. In the first place the general standard of
agriculture is not so high, and labour not so often procured from beyond the limits of the cultivator's familv
And in the second place the ties of hereditary occupation are infinitely more lax, so that a menial, u h i i i
he turns his attention to field-work, is not kept down in his place as a menial by custom and the fcch'ii"- ol
society; and instead of merely combining agricultural labour with his menial functions, as he would do in
the eastern half of the Panjib, he abandons the latter altogether and becomes a cultivator pure and simple.
O n e would have expected to find scavengers and water-carriers espec ially abundant on the lYsh.lwar Irontier, where the feeling about the seclusion of women is stronger than elsewhere. But so far as the vilke.es
are concerned this is not the case, and it appears that Pathan women enjoy consiehTable liberty within the
limits of their own village. Mr. Beckett explains the small number ol si avengers returned from the
Peshawar district by pointing out that the scavengers of those parts ordinarily (lean and dress grain as one
of their occupations; but this only accounts for a very small part of the deli( ii nc y. The carpenters and
blacksmiths, who often can hardly be separated the one from the other, are found in fairh constant n u m b e r
throughout the Province; though here again the numbers are smaller in the western districts win -n-soc h ty
is less highly organised, wealth is less, and the needs of the people more simple. Pollers an- natural!)
found in largest numbers where irrigation from wells is most largely praclised.
734. In the towns the village menials whom I have just discussed an- hardly to he distinguished from
the other artisans save by difference of calling; for except in so far as they serve the village communities
which are attached to most of the smaller towns, they are paid by the job or by the day like the other industrial classes, and are independent of the outturn of the harvest. The variations in the proportion they
bear to the urban population are naturally much smaller than in the case of villages, though the c auses just
described which affect the latter are not without effect on the tow 11 population also. 'I he scavengers and
water-carriers especially are most numerous where great cities contain large numbers of the higher and
more wealthy classes, who are particular about the seclusion of their women and can allord to pay for the
rendering of the necessary services.
735. T h e workers in fabrics and dress.—The next group in Abstract No. 122, page 3X0, includes all tho
workers and dealers in wool, pashm, cotton, and silk, and the washermen and dyers. It corresponds with
order i t of the tables, with the exclusion of shoe-makers and barbers. Of the classes included in this group
the only two who are at all numerously represented among the village population are the cotton-weavers
and the dyers, while even in the towns these two constitute the greater portion of the group. Tinweavers can hardly be separated from the leather-workers, many of whom add weaving to their more proper calling ; and accordingly we find weavers proper scantily represented in the eastern districts where
leather-workers are most numerous. The dyers and washermen are fairly equally distributed, except in
the Multan division where they are curiously numerous and in Amritsar where they are engaged in tingreat industries of that city. Among the villages washermen are almost confined to those parts whenlocal custom forbids respectable women to wash the clothes of their families. The cotton-c h aners are very
evenly distributed, though again most numerous in the Mulbin division. The /»tf.\7//j/-workers are c hielly
confined to the towns of Amritsar, Ludhidna, and the Rawalpindi division; and the drapers and < -mbroiderers, the other workers in dress, and indeed the whole group, are most numerous in Amritsar whic h is tingreat centre of shawl-making and embroidery in the Panj.lb. and the entries under these four occupations comprise nearly forty per cent, of the non-agricultural occupations returned for women. But if a woman returned her domestic work as an occupation she would
almost certainly use one of these four expressions by which to describe it, and consequently we cannot
be certain that some at least of the entries under these heads do not refer to domestic occupations which
should not have been entered at all. The third form.of error which is to be apprehended is that in which
the woman, though really assisting the males of the family in their callings, has, whether from negligence
or from a wish to make it appear that she is under no necessity to work for her living, had no occupation
entered for her, thus implying that she is engaged wholly in domestic duties; and this has I fear been
the case in very many instances.
744. T h e a g r i c u l t u r a l o c c u p a t i o n s Of w o m e n . — I t is a most difficult thing to decide what women
should be returned as agriculturists, that is to say as actually assisting in cultivation.* It is possible to
distinguish four grades between the woman who never goes near her husband's'field, and the woman who
works in it almost as hard as he does himself. W e have first the classes among whom the women are
strictly secluded, and here of course they render no assistance whatever. But among all the classes who
do not strictly seclude their women, and in the poorer families of even those classes who do ordinarily
seclude their women, the wife almost invariably takes the midday meal to the men who are at work in
the fields, and will commonly pick and carry back a few pot herbs for dinner or a little fresh grain for
frumenty. The third grade is where the women, besides carrying the food, pick cotton and safllower,
carry fodder, and do light field-work of all sorts, perhaps helping the reapers also at harvest. And
finally there are classes among whom the women work if anything harder than the- men, all the weeding
and much of the hoeing being done by them, while ploughing and sowing, for which latter operation a
woman is incapacitated by her sex, are the only two branches of agricultural labour in which they take
no share 1 . The first and fourth classes are sufficiently well marked; but between them tin-re is room
for great variety of practice, and for no less difference of opinion as to what degree of assistance rendered
would justify a woman in recording her occupation as agricultural.
745. Now the practice of the women in this respect is very largely a matter of tribal custom, their
abstention from field-work being looked upon as in some respects a mark ol higher social status. Hut it
is not wholly regulated by such custom ; and while poverty will sometimes compel women who from their
caste would not be expected to work in the fields to do so, it is still more commonly the case that social
pride and pretensions induce sections of those castes whose women ordinarily do field-work of all sorts to
affect the exclusiveness of the higher castes. And the practice varies from one part ol the Province to
another, and in some parts from tribe to tribe of the same caste, from village to village of the
same tribe, and even from family to family of the same village. In the eastern and south-eastern districts
the practice is fairly uniform. The women of Jats and Rors, and of Kambohs, Arains, and similar minor
agricultural tribes, work regularly with the men in the fields; the women of the richer Brahmans, Tagas,
Saiyads, and Rajputs do not go into the fields at all; while those of the poorer families of these castes and
of all Gujars merely do light field-work, and even that not as a daily occupation. In the hills the women
of all but Brahmans and Rajputs work in the fields, while in the higher Himalayas almost the whole o( the
field-work, not always excepting ploughing, is done by the women, the men working meanwhile as carriers,
coolies, and the like. On the frontier the Pathan women work very generally in the fields, but not as a
rule till they are some 25 years old, and then only at the lighter kinds of labour and at harvest time.
Throughout the greater part of the Province the women of the Arains, Sainis, Malis, and similar inferior
castes work with their husbands in the fields; but in the Western Plains even these women, and still more
those of the higher classes, take very little part in agriculture. Finally in the central and Sikh tracts and in
the adjoining sub-montane, while the women of Gujars do light field work, those of Jats hardly ever help in
the cultivation. When Mr. Elliott who came from the North-West Provinces, and I who knew only the Jamna
districts, went through the Panjab on a tour of inspection, we could hardly believe it possible thai the women
of Jat households should not ordinarily be recorded as assisting in agriculture. But there is no doubt ol the
fact that, unlike their sisters of Hindustan whose agricultural industry has become proverbial, the Jat women
of the Panjab proper do not ordinarily assist their men in the work of cultivation. The difference is doubtless due to the far higher social and political status enjoyed by the Jat in the stronghold of the Sikh
Khalsa than in parts where other tribes occupy a dominant position.
746. The variety of practice being so great and the gradations so many, and there being, as Mr.
Kensington puts it in writing of Hushyarpur, " a natural delicacy in admitting that the women work in
" t h e fields," it is hardly to be expected that our record of female agriculturists should be even approximately
complete, or that the figures should have any very definite significance. And besides the wives ol the husbandmen themselves, all the women of the village menial class almost without exception do field-work for
hire at seasons, such as harvest time, when the work must be done quickly and extra labour is needed ;
while where the better class of women take no part in the cultivation, the whole of the cotton and safllower
picking and of such weeding as is done at all, is done by these menial women for payment. Thus while
this class of females perform on the whole a very considerable amount of agricultural labour, it can hardly
be said that they are cultivators by occupation, for it is only at certain seasons that their services are required.

cultivator. I suspect that the former figures are slightly and the latter very largely below the truth. But it
is probable that the sequence of the divisions is very nearly in accordance with the facts, and that the proportion of females who do field work is largest in the eastern and south-eastern districts, next largest in the
hills and sub-montane, then in the Salt-range Tract, still smaller in the central and frontier districts, and
smallest of all in the districts of the Western Plains.

:8

748- Non-agricultural occupations of females.—The extraordinary variation in the numbers of
female cultivators returned from the several divisions renders any comparison between the figures for other
occupations shown in Abstract No. 125 for the various divisions almost meaningless. Since 50 per cent, of
the whole are agricultural in the Dehli and only 5 per cent, in the Lahore division, the figures for an occupation w;hich bore the same proportion in both divisions to the total of non-agricultural occupations would
be by mere arithmetical consequence nearly double in the latter what they would be in the former; and
I have just explained why proportions to total population would be unsatisfactory. The occupations of
women are noticed in detail under their several headings in the second part of this chapter, and I shall
here do nothing more than briefly note their distribution in the Province taking it as a whole. In summing up the distribution of occupations in section 752, I shall give the proportions which the main groups
of female occupations bear to the total adult female population.
T h e occupations may be roughly classed under two heads, those in which the women simply assist
their fathers and husbands in their work, and those which are female occupations proper where the whole
work is done by the women. Of course it is not always possible to class any given occupation wholly
under either head. T o the first kind of occupations belong all the female cultivators, who constitute some
40 per cent, of the whole. It may be that a certain number of women have been wrongly returned as landowners who do not cultivate themselves, but this error has probably been rare. A woman cultivating on
her own account, that is to say unassisted by men, is I believe quite unknown in the Panjdb unless
it be in the higher hills. Under this head fall also the workers in leather, who probably help in curino- and
dyeing leather and perhaps in the lighter kinds of sewing. The women returned as blacksmiths probably
do little more than blow the bellows, and their nurrfber is small ; though the women of the vagrant or
GAdiya Lohirs commonly wield the forehammer. The female potters perhaps mould the clay, while
the female oil-pressers may drive the bullocks. The total of these classes is under 5 per cent, of the
whole, and it is probable that in some cases at any rate the women have been shown as following the occupation of their husbands through carelessness, rather than because thev really assist them in their calling.
The female weavers comprise 6£ per cent, of the total, and the numbers are, as noted bv several Deputv
Commissioners, probably very much below the truth. The women of the weaver classes prepare the web
and fill the spools ready for the weavers' hand, and are an important element in the industry ; though perhaps but a small number are wholly occupied in these occupations. The female cotton scutchers are
chiefly occupied in rolling into rolls ready for spinning the cotton scutched by their husbands. Thus the
women who merely help the men constitute almost exactly the half of the total women whose occupation
is recorded, about 40 per cent, being cultivators and 10 per cent, artisans. These women follow the fortunes of their families, and thrive or starve with them.
749. But the women who follow occupations which can be wholly performed by females, while perhaps
in the majority of instances they have husbands or sons whose income they help to increase, are in very
many cases, and especially in the cities, poor widows or forlorn women who have nothing but their own
labour to depend upon and who often find the greatest difficulty in earning a bare subsistence. These women
very generally employ themselves in spinning cotton and grinding corn, especially if thev belong to the
higher castes, as these are in-door occupations, and in working as coolies if they belong to classes who are
not secluded. The cotton spinners form 13, the corn-grinders 6£, and the coolies 3 ^ per cent, of the
whole; though as before remarked corn-grinding and cotton-spinning, like water-carrying and cooking, may
in some cases have been wrongly returned as generic terms for mere domestic duties.
T h e r e remains about 25 per cent, of the female occupations to be accounted for. The water-carriers,
cooks, scavengers, and washerwomen form n per cent, of the whole. These women an.- verv generally employed to bring water, remove night-soil, and wash clothes in houses where the females are
strictly secluded; while the cooks are in some cases domestic servants, but more common I v keep public
bakeries and cook for the village. In the villages they are perhaps generally village menials r e c e m n g
customary dues, often taking the form of a fixed share of the produce; but elsewhere they depend upon the
wealthier classes for their income, which though scanty is tolerably secure. The female money-lenders are
probably women who have either been returned wrongly as following the occupation of their hn.-bands.
or who own capital and lend it through agents ; but nearly half the female mercantile class consists o\ peity
hawkers and pedlars, who like the greengrocers and costermongersare generally miserably poor. These two

LChap. VIII.

Part I.—General and Comparative.
Besides these cultivating menials, other village menials paid for the most part by receiving a share of the
-produce constitute another 6 per c e n t . ; so that not less than 73 per cent, of the whole village population, and at the very least 16 per cent, of the town population, depend almost if not quite entirely for their
subsistence upon the varying nature of the seasons and upon the produce of the fields. Of the remaining
village population 3 per cent, are priests and professional men whose income also depends largely upon a
favourable harvest, 5 per cent, belong to the mercantile and money-lending class whose livelihood is comparatively secure, 7 per cent, are artisans such as weavers and the like, whose income is always small but
not directly dependent upon the seasons, though distress and high prices must always affect soonest the
poorest classes, while 4 per cent, are coolies and day-labourers dependent for bare subsistence upon each
day's chances, and another 4 per cent, are beggars and faqirs.
Government and domestic service account
for the remaining 3 per cent.
Of the adult male populationof the towns 16 per cent, are purely agricultural and pastoral, while a
considerable proportion of the menials in the smaller towns are paid according to the outturn of the harvest. Some \o\ per cent.belong to the mercantile, 2 J per cent, to the carrying, and 3 per cent, to the priestly and professional classes, all of whom are tolerably secure of their livelihood, as are most of the 4^ per cent.
who work and deal in articles of food. Government and domestic service provide employment for \~j\ per
cent., while about 8 per cent are menials who are chiefly employed in serving the wealthier classes, and are
not so wholly dependent as many others upon the fluctuations of trade and of the labour market. Ordinary artisans constitute I2£ per cent, of the whole, and are as a rule comfortably off according to their position in life, but the weaving classes who comprise 8 per cent, more are often miserably poor. The day labourers who are seldom certain of a day's food in advance constitute 10 per cent, of the whole urban population, while the faqirs and beggars amount to 4 per cent, more, leaving only 3 ! per cent, unaccounted for.
752. Of the total.female population over 15 years of age, 76 per cent, have had no occupations returned for them and must be supposed to be chiefly employed in domestic duties, though the numbers who are
compelled to earn their own living either wholly or in part are probably much larger than would appear
from these figures. In stating the composition of the remaining 24 per cent, of the adult female population
I shall first give the percentages following each occupation calculated upon that 24 per cent, only, and shall
add in brackets the corresponding percentage calculated upon the total adult female population. Of the
women for whom occupations are recorded, 3 9 ! per cent. (9/4) assist their husbands in cultivation, and 6
per cent. (1'4) in industrial occupations. Minor branches of the weaving trade employ 6 | per cent. (15)
more, domestic service and attendance upon the wealthier classes occupy 11 per cent. (26J of the whole,
while 2A P e r cent. (o'8) follow professional pursuits. The remaining 33I per cent. (80) of the female population of towns are miserably poor, and earn their bread by daily labour of the most uncertain kind, 15
per cent. (36) by spinning, 12^ per cent. (30) by general labour such as gathering cowdung, grass, or
fuel, or working as common coolies, and 4^ per cent. (11) by begging.
The children of course share the fortunes of their parents. Those of the poorer classes are set to work
as soon as they have the necessary intelligence, while the children of husbandmen tend cattle and perform
similar light duties from a very early age. As they grow older the work becomes harder, till they enter
into the full inheritance of that almost incessant though not always very arduous toil which is the lot of the
immense majority of the population of the Panjab.
753. Concluding remarks.—I am only too conscious how hasty and imperfect is the above sketch of
t h e occupations of the people. But without the district figures it was impossible to enter into details ; while
even had they been available, the system of classification adopted has so obscured their meaning that it
would hardly have been worth while to examine them very minutely. I have discussed the composition
and significance of the figures under each heading of the tables with some fullness in the succeeding portion
of this chapter, and I hope that with the aid of those remarks the figures will furnish such information as
may b e needed for general purposes of administration. But they will not serve the purpose of detailed
inquiry into the constitution of particular industries, and I doubt whether any record of occupations made
at a general Census in this country would suffice for such a purpose. In discussing the figures in Part II of
the chapter, I have noticed many minor occupations which are interesting rather from their singular nature
than because of their industrial importance. I have however given little or no information regarding the
processes or appliances of the industries discussed. A great deal of most valuable matter will be found in
Mr. Baden-Powell's Panjab Products and Panjab Manufactures
and in Mr. Hoey's monograph on the
Trade and Manufactures
of Northern India.
Some information regarding the grouping of occupations
will be found in the chapter of this Report which deals with castes, and especially in the last part of that
chapter. I have not attempted to institute any comparison between the figures of the last and those of the
present Census ; indeed any such comparison would be wholly impossible.
In the first place the results
were classified in 1868 on a somewhat different system from that now adopted, while there is not the
slightest indication of how details were grouped, or whether any uniform system of grouping was followed ;
indeed the figures show conclusively that the want of uniformity was far greater than even that which our
present figures display. But the chief reason which renders comparison impossible is that, whereas we
show in our tables only the effective number engaged in the prosecution of each industry, the figures of
1868 represented the total number dependent for their living upon each industry, and included children of
tender age; which our figures exclude.

is advisable, Tbe canal staff especially may even include mere labourers returned as in the service of the Ciinal Department. It
is worthy of consideration also whether doctors, teachers, and the like who are in the service of Government, should be shown under
their distinct occupations or as Government servants. If the latter, distinct directions should be ^ivon that every one who is a
Government servant should state the fact in specifying his occupalion. Many of the Government schoolmasters lor instance returned themselves simply as schoolmasters, and are not included among Government servants. On the other hand, the immense
majority of clerks and munBbia returned themselves simply as such, without specifying the occupation ot' their masters. This

S^nsis and 324 Nats, the former of whom might perhaps have been classed as workers in grass or hunters, and the latter as tumblers.
The prisoners ^No. 329) were returned as such, and not by their original occupations, under the orders of the Government of India.
That so many of them are returned in some districts from the villages, is due to the fact that the gaol sometimes lies outside the
boundaries of civil lines, as is the case with the Lahore Central Gaol. Some o£ course would be in the lock-ups in the district.
No rule was laid dotvn as to how prisoners awaiting trial were to be returned, and the practice has probably not been uniform.
The prostitute class (Nos. - 331, 332) has probably been understated; but most of the tumblers and dancing-girls are habitual
prostitutes. Finally under " O t h e r s " (No. 333) I have included 63 candidates for employment, 53 male and 16 female gamblers, 514
Saiyads, and 2 informers, 2 thieves, and 2 blackguards (badmdsh) returned as such, whether of their own motion or by a too wellinformed enumerator, I cannot tell.

EDUCATION IN THE PANJAB.

Education.

CHAPTER IX.

EDUCATION IN T H E PANJAB.
807a. .Introductory.—The figures for education are contained in Table XIII of Appendices A and B,
which shows the total numbers of each sex for all religions and for each religion separately, who are under
instruction and who are able to read and write, distinguishing rural from total population. It is probable
that the figures are less correct than any others, except those for age, obtained at the present Census ; or
if not absolutely less correct, are at any rate possessed of less, significance. The instructions issued to
enumerators were that nobody "who could not both read and write was to be shown as educated. It
is probable that these instructions were not always understood or carried out. Thus Mr. Anderson observes that of the 229 persons shown as educated in Spiti, it is to be feared that not a few could only read
and not"write; while in Siaikot it was found that some of the enumerators were entering as educated, only
such as could read, and write the Persian character. On the other hand, the instructions directed that all
under instruction should be so shown ; and this was obviously wrong. In the Musalman indigenous schools
of a religious character the boys are often taught to read only and not to write ; and such boys should not
have been included. It is probable also that boys still at school but who had learnt to read and write,
were occasionally entered as educated instead of as under instruction.
The figures for female education are probably still less accurate, for here there is a probability that
wrong returns were intentionally made. A native woman may be able to read ; but it is not fitting that a
respectable woman should be able to write, that accomplishment being reserved for women of light charact e r . It is not " good form," and there would be a disinclination on the part of the people to admit that
their wives and daughters could both read and write, even when they could do so.
Again, supposing that the instructions were rightly understood, and that there was no tendency to
conceal facts, there are so many degrees of " r e a d i n g and writing" that it must often have been difficult to
decide how a man should be entered. In the Jamna districts for instance, very many of the village headmen can read the Mahajani, or as they call it Hindi character, and can write their names in it, and perhaps make shift t o painfully scrawl any word set them. But for all practical purposes of ready writing
they are illiterate. Just before the Census was taken, Mr. Tolbort proposed to enter in the column for
education, instead of the words " c a n read and write," the name of the character with which he was acquainted before the name of each'person who could read and write. The proposal came too late for action ;
but I am not at all sure that it was not a good one. It would increase the labour of tabulation ; but the
difference in the degree of education that is implied by the ability to read and write the Persian and Mahajani characters respectively is often immense ; and if the information were collected at successive enumerations the figures would throw great light upon the progress of education in the Province.

Chap. IX. J

EDUCATION IN THE PANJAB.

Education.
Colonel Holroyd's figures for Government schools are taken from the returns for 1880-81; but those
for the attendance at indigenous schools are only a rough estimate made in 1879-80 after local enquiry.
For males, my figures compare well with his on the whole. In the Peshawar and Rawalpindi divisions,
where the Mahomedans are most bigoted and the Quran schools at which boys are not taught to write
most numerous, my figures are in deficit; and this is as it should be, for his figures include, and mine
should not, the attendance at such schools. Indeed either my figures or his estimate must be wrong for
Peshawar ; probably the latter, judging by comparison with neighbouring districts. It is hardly probable
that Peshawar, with a population half as large again as that of Hazara and more than three times that
of Kohat, should have only 2,000 indigenous scholars against 4,731 and 1,330 respectively. In other
districts my figures are in e x c e s s ; and this again is as it should be, for my figures include private tuition
which Colonel Holroyd's do not.
As for females, Colonel Holroyd's figures are actuals, not estimates, and mine must be utterly worthless. I have already assigned a reason for their being so.

809. State of education in various parts of the Province.—Abstract No. 128 on the opposite pao-e

shows the educated proportion per 10,000 of the population of each District and State, those districts
being put first in which education has made greatest progress among the total male population.
With the exception of the hilly districts of Hazara and Kohat and the district of Gujrat, the frontier
districts and those of the Multan and Rawalpindi divisions stand very high on the list. The three
exceptions will be seen on referring to Abstract No. 127 (page 401,) to be those districts in which my figures
fall far short of the estimate of the Educational D e p a r t m e n t ; and it is to be feared that the apparent pre-eminence of the western districts is due to the fact that, except in Hazara, Kohat and Gujrat, boys
attending the Quran schools so numerous in the west, and learning to read only and not to write, and adults
who have been so trained, have been included in our figures. Next to the western districts come the
median districts and the northern zone of the Eastern Plains, including the commercial and military centres of
Lahore, Amritsar, Jalandhar, Kangra and Ludhianah. Gujranwala stands very high, and so does the little
State of Pataudi. Well at the bottom of the list come the Hill States, the minor States of the Eastern Plains,
HissSr, Karnal and Gurgaon, Hazara and Kohat, Gujrat, Bannu and Bahawalpur; while in the middle stand
Dehli, Patiala and Nabha, Rohtak and Sirsa, the sub-montane districts except Hushvarpur which is hicrh,
and Firozpur. Generally it m a y b e said that, taking the figures as they stand and remembering that they
probably include the schools of the Mullas, education is highest in the west and after that in the central
districts, partly no doubt because these districts contain the great proportion of the military forces of the
P a n j a b ; and lowest in the hills, the sub-montane districts, and the central and southern portions of
the Eastern Plains. The districts which include the great cities and cantonments naturally stand hio-h j n
comparison with their neighbours.
Taking rural populations only, Peshawar, Amritsar and Lahore sink at once and markedly in the list ;
while Montgomery, Patiala, Nabha, Rohtak, Kangra, and the sub-montane districts rise.
T h e figures for female education are obscured by the inclusion of Christians, which constitute a fourth
of the whole; and it would have been better had I excluded Christians from my statistics. But omittin^
cantonments, Gujranwala, Jhang, Shahpur and Ludhianah stand high, while the figures for Suket and Bhajfi
and still more for Keonthal are, if accurate, extraordinarily large.

,
T h e pre-eminence of the Jains is very striking, but also very natural. They consist almost wholly of
the mercantile classes, and very largely of the wealthiest portions of those classes, and indeed I am inclined
to think that the figures must be very much understated. There are out of every 10,000 Jains over 6,500
who are above 15 years of age, and a very small proportion of these can be'still at school. Yet it is
difficult to believe that more than 2,800 of them cannot read and write. It is possible that in some places,
as already suggested, only such as could read and write the Persian character were returned as educated.
At any rate whatever the nature of the error may be, I do not believe that the figures are correct ; nor do 1
believe that only 650 out of the 1,160 children between 10 and 15 years of age which are found anion" every
10,000 Jains are under instruction.

L Chap. IX.

EDUCATION IN THE PANJAB.

Education.
The Buddhists come n e x t ; but here Mr. Anderson's qualification must b e r e m e m b e r e d that probably
very many of these men can only read and not write. The monks which almost every Spiti family contains
are taught to read in the monasteries ; but as a rule they do not learn to write also. Mr. Anderson writes
thus of education in Lahul and S p i t i : " In Lahul a comparatively large number can read and write
" Tankri, Pahari, and also Tibetan. Education is more advanced there than in Kulu. The Lamas can all read
" the printed character, but they are not all able to write Tibetan. They do not as a rule know Tankri.
" T h e traders know both'Tankri and Tibetan. The fact of the Lahulis engaging generally in trade both with
'* KiSIu and with Ladakh and Tibet, may explain why the d e m e n t s of education are more widespread among
" them than in Kulu. There is only one school in Lahul, and in it both Urdu and Tibetan are taught. Before
" b o y s are admitted into the Urdu classes they have to pass through a course in Tibetan. Still here, as in
" Kulu, education is considered a species of begar (forced labour), and the father expects to be exempted
" from carrying loads, & c , while his son is at school. In Kulu there are two schools ; but they would have
" very few scholars were not the parents encouraged by exemption from begdr to send their children. Educ a t i o n in Spiti is at its lowest. Few can read and fewer still can write. Urdu is unknown, and an inter.
" preter is kept to carry out or translate for the benefit of the headmen the few orders that relate to that
" part of the sub-division. There is no school in Spiti."

ill

Next to them come the Hindus, and here again their comparatively high position is due to the large
proportion of them engaged in commerce, especially in the towns. The proportion of Hindus at school or
already educated steadily rises from one division to another as the generally Hindu character of the population d e c r e a s e s ; it is lowest in Dehli and the Hill States where Hinduism is most prevalent, and highest
on the frontier where Hinduism is least general ; and this is due to the fact that wherever the general population is Musalman, the Hindus belong almost entirely to the mercantile classes. The proportion is naturally greater in the towns where commerce is most rife; and the difference between town and village is
largest in this respect where Hinduism is most common, and where therefore the largest proportion of the
rural Hindu population is agricultural.
Next follow the Sikhs, an almost purely agricultural and artisan population, with not much more than
half the percentage for Hindus, and still less than that in the specially Sikh t r a c t s ; and here again the
same points are observable as with the Hindus, for in the parts where Sikhs are few many of them are
educated Khatris. Last of all come the Musalmans with a uniformly low proportion of educated among
-the villages, but a much higher proportion in

wholly illiterate, come the Hindus. But the most encouraging feature of the figures, if they are even approximately correct, is the proportion of scholars to educated adults, which would seem to show that the
education of women is really making progress in the new generation. There are about three times as
many "women over 15 years of age as there are girls between 5 and 15; and even on the exaggerated
assumption that the ordinary schooling of a native girl lasts from 5 to 15, if 8'g per 10,000 of the grownup women can read and write, only 2-97 should at the same rate be under instruction. Instead of this there
are 6-3, or more than twice as many as there should be. In other words, education is twice as general
among the girls of 5 to 15 years of age as it is among the women of over 15 years. The figures are small
a t the b e s t ; b u t so far as they may be trusted they show distinct progress.
